title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
author: Nilay Patel

This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life. I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security. summary.tldr:
Alex Stamos, Chief Security Officer at Cognition and lecturer at the Stanford University Cyber Policy Center, argues that the current multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry is fundamentally ill-equipped to handle the surge in AI-augmented cyberattacks. Stamos characterizes the current landscape as a 'dark age' of security, noting that both private and state-sponsored actors—specifically citing Russia and North Korea—are leveraging AI to simultaneously detect and exploit system vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale.

Stamos draws parallels between the current environment and the 1990s, describing a 'frontier' atmosphere where rapid technological disruption outpaces defensive capabilities. The discussion highlights that AI is not only facilitating technical breaches but also complicating the management of misinformation and automated content on social networks. Stamos suggests that the industry is currently in a period of reactive scrambling, necessitating a significant shift in how organizations approach cyber defense in an era where AI-driven threats are becoming the standard.
takeaways: **Industry Outlook:** Alex Stamos asserts that the existing cybersecurity industry model is overdue for a collapse due to the unrelenting nature of AI-boosted attacks.
**Threat Actors:** State-sponsored entities, including Russia and North Korea, are actively utilizing AI to automate the discovery and exploitation of system vulnerabilities.
**Historical Context:** The current cybersecurity landscape is compared to the 1990s, characterized by a 'frontier' environment where rapid, disruptive change leaves systems highly vulnerable.
**Scope of Impact:** The disruption extends beyond traditional network security to include the management of AI-powered misinformation and automated content on social media platforms.

title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
author: Robert Hart
contentSnippet: Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down. That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer. The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development. But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development. Here are some of the biggest takeaways. AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress. Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. summary.tldr:
A new investigation published by the AI safety research organization METR reveals that Anthropic's AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they did a year ago, achieving an estimated two years of historical progress in a single year. Following an 11-week probe inside the company, METR concluded that the majority of this acceleration is driven by AI assistance rather than increases in raw compute scaling. Employees utilizing Anthropic's most capable internal models reported being on average 12 times more productive than without AI assistance. The findings highlight a growing trend of AI accelerating its own development, raising critical questions about recursive self-improvement and the timeline for autonomous AI R&D.

Despite granting METR access to confidential research, model data, and employee interviews, Anthropic exercised extensive editorial control over the final publication. The company redacted the majority of the most informative evidence from METR's roughly 100-page report, citing commercial sensitivity and the risk of providing rivals with a competitive roadmap. Co-founder Sam McCandlish defended the redactions on X, noting that while it complicates external verification, Anthropic plans to publish its own report on progress speeds and safety measures. Meanwhile, METR documented three unreleased internal models—codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4—that completed training consecutively between July and October, alongside an older 2022 model.
takeaways: **METR Investigation Findings:** AI safety organization METR published a report following an 11-week investigation detailing how Anthropic's models are improving twice as quickly as a year ago, equating to roughly two years of historical progress in twelve months.
**Compute vs. AI Contribution:** METR researchers expressed high confidence that the acceleration is primarily driven by AI-assisted R&D rather than historical drivers like increased compute scaling.

**Employee Productivity Metrics:** Internal Slack polls and interviews showed that Anthropic employees using the lab's most capable internal model self-reported being roughly 12 times more productive, double the rate reported a few months prior with Mythos 5.

**Unreleased Model Pipeline:** METR identified three unreleased models trained over recent months—Model 2 (completed July), Model 3 (August-September), and Model 4 (September-October)—plus an older internal model called Unreleased 2022.

**Extensive Redactions:** Anthropic heavily redacted the public version of METR's 100-page report to protect commercially sensitive data and prevent handing competitors a development roadmap, according to co-founder Sam McCandlish.

title: Buoyant Releases Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for Kubernetes and vLLM
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Buoyant, the company behind Linkerd, has released Kinference , an open source project for building inference platforms on Kubernetes. Kinference is an inference control plane for Kubernetes and vLLM. It sits in front of a fleet of vLLM workers and decides where each request goes. It applies routing policies, token rate limits, KV-cache-aware load balancing and per-tenant metrics in one layer. For dev teams serving many open-weight models to many internal clients, it targets the layer above the model server. The project is Apache 2.0 licensed on GitHub . The current release is v0.1.0-alpha.7 . TL;DR Size: v0.1.0-alpha.7, written in Rust, Apache 2.0, configured through 5 Kubernetes CRDs. Runs on: any GPU-enabled Kubernetes cluster running vLLM. Buoyant’s benchmark used 3 L40S GPUs per pool. Performance: large gains on prefix-heavy traffic versus plain Kubernetes Service routing (self-reported). Best: median TTFT fell from 6.88 s to 0.31 s (95%) on a shared-prefix workload. Worst: no median TTFT gain on prompts without shared prefixes (6.92 s vs 6.83 s). What is Kinference? Kinference is a policy-driven control plane that turns Kubernetes plus vLLM into a multi-tenant inference platform. Buoyant’s FAQ puts it simply: vLLM is the data plane and Kinference is the control plane. How does Kinference work? The system has 2 parts: a traffic gateway and an inference handler. The GitHub README states that the handler exposes a gRPC interface. It takes a request and returns the chosen endpoint plus a possibly mutated body. It pairs with a proxy such as the Buoyant Gateway . Kinference watches vLLM KV-cache events and engine metrics. It currently uses NVIDIA’s dynamo-kv-router crate to process cache events. Configuration lives in 5 CRDs: GatewayBackend, InferencePolicy, InferencePool, InferenceProvider and InferenceWorkerSet . What are inference policies? Inference policies are declarative rules for how each request is routed or rejected. Rules can match on tenant, requested model, GPU pool state and semantic tags. Example policies on the project site cover 5 patterns: Simple to cheaper: route low-complexity prompts to a smaller model, unless cache overlap makes the large model faster. Burst to cloud: skip workers with over 2 queued prompts, then fall back to providers like Bedrock. PII stays local: remove external providers when a PII tag fires, and fail closed with onE

summary.tldr:
Buoyant, the creators of Linkerd, have launched Kinference, an open-source inference control plane designed to manage vLLM deployments on Kubernetes. Released under the Apache 2.0 license as version v0.1.0-alpha.7, the project is written in Rust and functions as a policy-driven orchestration layer that sits above model servers. It enables multi-tenant inference by providing KV-cache-aware load balancing, token rate limiting, and per-tenant metrics, effectively separating the control plane (Kinference) from the data plane (vLLM).

The architecture consists of a traffic gateway and an inference handler that exposes a gRPC interface, utilizing NVIDIA’s dynamo-kv-router crate to monitor engine metrics and KV-cache events. Configuration is managed through five custom Kubernetes CRDs: GatewayBackend, InferencePolicy, InferencePool, InferenceProvider, and InferenceWorkerSet. These allow for declarative routing based on tenant, model, GPU pool state, and semantic tags. Buoyant’s internal benchmarks on a 3-GPU L40S cluster demonstrated significant performance improvements for prefix-heavy workloads, with median Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) dropping from 6.88 seconds to 0.31 seconds. However, the system showed negligible performance gains for prompts lacking shared prefixes, where TTFT remained largely unchanged at approximately 6.9 seconds.
takeaways: **Architecture:** Kinference operates as a control plane using five specific Kubernetes CRDs to manage routing, policy, and worker sets.
**Performance:** Benchmarks on L40S GPUs showed a 95% reduction in median TTFT for shared-prefix workloads, but no significant improvement for non-prefix-heavy traffic.
**Technical Stack:** The project is written in Rust, utilizes gRPC for handler communication, and integrates with NVIDIA’s dynamo-kv-router for cache-aware routing.
**Policy Capabilities:** Supports complex routing logic, including cost-based routing, cloud bursting to providers like Bedrock, and PII-based local-only enforcement.

title: Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google
author: Marina Temkin
contentSnippet:
Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion , confirmed Friday it has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google.

Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over the development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management.

Crusoe initially announced the project last year with Blackstone-backed infrastructure company Tallgrass, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity.

Google did not disclose how much it paid Crusoe for the unfinished project, bu it announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus.

The deal highlights how difficult it can be for independent data center developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Growing opposition from local communities can further complicate development.

Despite taking over the Wyoming facility, Google hasn’t walked away from working with Crusoe entirely. Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.

The deal to sell the site to Google was first reported by Bloomberg in June, but the Wyoming setback didn’t stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion round in September.

Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.

Crusoe’s largest projects serve some of the biggest names in AI. Its campus in Abilene, Texas, is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and the company is also constructing a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft, with its first building expected to come online in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that the trading firm Jane Street signed a $13 billion , five-year cloud deal with Crusoe.

Crusoe was founded by Chase Lochmiller, now its CEO, and Cully Cavness, who started it as a cryptocurrency-mining business powered by natural gas that would otherwise have been burned off. In September, alongside its $3.9 billion funding round, the company added three board members , including JB Straubel, the Redwood Materials founder and Tesla board member who invested in Crusoe in 2021. summary.tldr:
Denver-based data center developer Crusoe has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google after failing to secure Google as a customer under its original management. Crusoe had initially announced the project last year alongside Blackstone-backed infrastructure firm Tallgrass, with plans to scale capacity up to 10 gigawatts. Google did not disclose the acquisition price paid to Crusoe but announced a $17 billion investment plan to develop the data center campus.

The transaction illustrates the acute challenges independent data center developers face in delivering massive infrastructure on schedule and within budget amid equipment, power procurement, and local community hurdles. Despite losing the Wyoming project, Google maintains a working relationship with Crusoe, which is developing another data center near Amarillo, Texas. Crusoe's broader infrastructure portfolio includes an Abilene, Texas campus being built for Oracle and OpenAI, a separate 900-megawatt campus for Microsoft targeting mid-2027 deployment, and a reported $13 billion, five-year cloud deal with trading firm Jane Street.

Founded by CEO Chase Lochmiller and Cully Cavness as a natural gas-powered crypto-mining operation utilizing flared gas, Crusoe recently closed a $3.9 billion funding round in September, elevating its valuation to $30.9 billion. The company's revenue streams span data center leasing for customer-owned GPUs, direct GPU rentals, and AI model inference compute sales.
takeaways: **Wyoming Project Acquisition:** Google took over Crusoe's unfinished southeastern Wyoming data center project after raising concerns over costs and construction timelines under Crusoe's management, committing a $17 billion investment to the campus.
**Original Scale Plans:** Crusoe initially announced the Wyoming project last year with Blackstone-backed Tallgrass, targeting an eventual power capacity scaling of 10 gigawatts.
**Massive Valuation and Funding:** Crusoe secured a $3.9 billion funding round in September, bringing its total valuation to $30.9 billion.

**Enterprise Infrastructure Pipeline:** Crusoe is constructing a multi-phase campus in Abilene, Texas for Oracle and OpenAI, a 900-megawatt campus for Microsoft (first building slated for mid-2027), and a reported $13 billion, five-year cloud agreement with Jane Street.

title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion. Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

summary.tldr:
OpenAI has achieved a $1.25 trillion valuation in a new funding round that secured $11 billion, according to Bloomberg reports. This follows a previous $122 billion investor raise in March at an $852 billion valuation. The company is reportedly pursuing additional investments to push the current round up to $20 billion, though it initially targeted raising up to $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation prior to a tech stock decline and midterms public opinion shifts against AI and data center projects.

Simultaneously, industry rival Anthropic filed its S-1 paperwork last week to prepare for an initial public offering. Meanwhile, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously stated that OpenAI is delaying its own IPO until it can make more confident claims regarding model safety, without providing a definitive timeline.
takeaways: **OpenAI Valuation:** Valued at $1.25 trillion following an $11 billion capital raise.
**Previous Funding:** Raised $122 billion from investors in March at an $852 billion valuation.
**Fundraising Targets:** Initially aimed to raise up to $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation before market pullbacks and political/public sentiment shifts.
**Competitive IPO Activity:** Rival company Anthropic filed its S-1 last week to go public.
**OpenAI IPO Stance:** CEO Sam Altman stated the company is holding off on going public until it has greater confidence in model safety claims.

title: OpenAI reportedly raises $11B in new funding at $1.25T valuation
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 18:43 EST / NOVEMBER 06 2026

OpenAI reportedly raises $11B in new funding at $1.25T valuation

OpenAI Group PBC has reportedly raised $11 billion as part of a funding round that could nearly double in size over the coming weeks, as s ources told Bloomberg that investors wired the funds to the company today.

The tipsters didn’t name the backers. The list of possible participants includes Microsoft Corp., which contributed to at least four of OpenAI’s previous rounds. That included its most recent $122 billion raise in March, which also drew the participation of Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and about two dozen others.

It’s believed that OpenAI could raise up to $9 billion in additional funding as part of the round. The deal is expected to value the company at $1.25 billion. That potentially puts it on track to surpass Anthropic PBC’s market capitalization.

Anthropic hopes to achieve a valuation of $1.5 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. However, several of its investors reportedly don’t consider that to be a realistic goal. According to the Wall Street Journal , one shareholder reportedly suggested that the company pursue a valuation closer to $1 trillion.

Anthropic’s IPO filing revealed that its quarterly revenue jumped 1,127% on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter. Last month, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI closed the quarter with $50 billion in net annualized revenue, which represented a 77% year-over-year increase. The company’s growth was driven by its enterprise business, which saw sales more than double.

The latest addition to OpenAI’s enterprise portfolio debuted on Thursday. GPT-6 Cyber can perform most cybersecurity tasks better than GPT-6 Astra, the company’s most capable general-purpose model. OpenAI engineers used it to develop 948 Linux⁠ exploits and uncover 81 high-severity zero-day flaws in Firefox.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman revealed on Wednesday that the company had experienced a slowdown in the first half of the year. Its growth started accelerating after the June launch of GPT-5.6 Sol, the immediate predecessor to GPT-6 Astra. Brockman added that OpenAI’s ChatGPT Work productivity application and coding tools played a role as well.

The company plans to go public sometime in 2027. Today’s cash infusion should make it easier for OpenAI to finance its steep infrastructure expenses until the

summary.tldr:
OpenAI Group PBC has reportedly raised $11 billion in new funding, with sources indicating the round could expand by an additional $9 billion and value the company at $1.25 trillion. The round follows previous participation from backers like Microsoft, Nvidia, and Amazon, providing financial runway ahead of an anticipated 2027 initial public offering. The capital injection comes as OpenAI manages over $665 billion in chip and data center commitments, alongside the development of a custom inference accelerator built in collaboration with Broadcom Inc. to reduce long-term infrastructure expenses.

Simultaneously, rival Anthropic PBC is preparing for its own IPO roadmap, targeting a public debut before Thanksgiving with hopes of achieving a $1.5 trillion valuation, though some investors suggest a $1 trillion target is more realistic. Financially, Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue growth of 1,127% year-over-year, while OpenAI closed the quarter with $50 billion in net annualized revenue—a 77% year-over-year increase driven primarily by its enterprise segment. Product milestones include the launch of GPT-6 Cyber, a specialized cybersecurity model used by engineers to construct 948 Linux exploits and uncover 81 high-severity zero-day Firefox vulnerabilities, alongside the broader market impact of GPT-5.6 Sol introduced in June.
takeaways: **OpenAI Funding & Valuation:** OpenAI raised $11 billion in new funding with potential to add $9 billion more, driving its valuation to $1.25 trillion ahead of a planned 2027 IPO.
**Infrastructure & Hardware Commitments:** OpenAI holds over $665 billion in data center and chip commitments and partnered with Broadcom Inc. to build a custom inference accelerator.
**Revenue Metrics:** OpenAI reported $50 billion in net annualized revenue for the quarter (a 77% year-over-year increase), while Anthropic posted Q3 revenue up 1,127% year-over-year.
**Model Capabilities:** GPT-6 Cyber was introduced for cybersecurity tasks, utilized by engineers to build 948 Linux exploits and find 81 high-severity zero-day flaws in Firefox.
**Anthropic IPO Plans:** Anthropic is planning to initiate its IPO roadmap ahead of Thanksgiving, aiming for a $1.5 trillion valuation despite pushback from investors favoring a $1 trillion target.

title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
author: Jay Peters
contentSnippet: China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says. Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new. The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

summary.tldr:
China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to reports by The New York Times. The intelligence operation aimed to extract information regarding American AI chips and pressure Nvidia into making its most advanced hardware accessible to China.

Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, maintained a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO and possessed professional ties with top executives across the AI chip industry, including leadership at Gigabyte. Megaspeed operates as a customer of Nvidia.

Former President Donald Trump received a briefing on the relationship last year but took no action. Following the publication of these intelligence findings, three House committees formally requested Jensen Huang to attend a joint, closed-door briefing concerning his interactions with Alice Huang.
takeaways: **Recruiting Agency:** China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted Megaspeed executive Alice Huang for espionage.
**Espionage Targets:** Objectives included gathering data on U.S. AI chips and influencing Nvidia to supply advanced chips to China.
**Industry Connections:** Alice Huang maintained close ties with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and executives at Gigabyte.
**Congressional Action:** Three House committees summoned Jensen Huang for a joint, closed-door briefing regarding his interactions with Alice Huang.

title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet:
Posted: 2:53 PM PST · November 6, 2026 Image Credits: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images Lucas Ropek OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.

In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.

TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.

OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market , with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

summary.tldr:
OpenAI has reportedly secured $11 billion in a new, ongoing funding round that values the company at $1.25 trillion. While the round remains open and is expected to close in the coming weeks, current projections suggest the total raise may reach approximately $20 billion. This figure represents a significant shortfall from the $30 billion target the company was reportedly pursuing as of late September.

The capital raise occurs amidst a cooling market for AI investments and heightened regulatory uncertainty. Concurrently, OpenAI’s primary competitor, Anthropic, is facing downward pressure on its own valuation ahead of a potential IPO. While investors previously anticipated a $2 trillion valuation for Anthropic, recent reports indicate that potential buyers are now eyeing a valuation as low as $1.1 trillion. OpenAI, which previously signaled intentions to go public in 2024 before delaying those plans, is now widely expected to pursue an IPO in 2025.
takeaways: **Current Funding Status:** OpenAI has raised $11 billion in a round expected to reach $20 billion total.
**Valuation:** The company is currently valued at $1.25 trillion.
**Market Comparison:** Anthropic's potential IPO valuation has reportedly dropped from an expected $2 trillion to approximately $1.1 trillion.
**IPO Timeline:** OpenAI has delayed its initial public offering plans, with expectations now shifted to 2025.
**Market Sentiment:** Investor confidence is currently impacted by political shifts following the U.S. midterms and public opposition to data center expansion.

title: Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 16:27 EST / NOVEMBER 06 2026

Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push

Thinking Machines Labs Inc. has released a new large language model that can automate artificial intelligence training tasks.

The algorithm, Inkling 2 Small, made its debut late Thursday. Around the same time, Business Insider reported that Thinking Machine is in the process of raising a $5 billion funding round led by Accel. The company, which was founded last year by former OpenAI Group PBC Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, is expected to receive a $40 billion valuation.

Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Small on a cluster of GB300 NVL72 racks. Each system contains 72 Blackwell Ultra graphics cards and half as many central processing units. The company completed the initial pre-training phase in 68 hours and subsequently refined the model through a nine-day reinforcement learning workflow. There were also a number of intermediate training steps.

Thinking Machines honed Inkling 2 Small’s programming capabilities by giving it hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding challenges. The task collection included a number of particularly complicated “autoresearch” exercises. They required the model to post-train neural networks, optimize LLM components called kernels and perform other AI research work.

Thinking Machines put Inkling 2 Small’s machine learning skills to the test by asking it to fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B. The goal was to improve the open-source LLM’s ability to make predictions such as weather forecasts. According to the company, Inking 2 Small doubled the model’s forecasting score in 4.5 hours.

The LLM is also adapt at automating business tasks. It outperformed Spark Open, Kimi K3 and several other open-source models on three popular knowledge work benchmarks. Additionally, it earned higher scores across several financial task datasets.

Inkling 2 Small includes a vision encoder that can analyze images. Moreover, it enables the LLM to visually verify the quality of the graphics that it generates. If a user asks the model to create an e-commerce store, it can not only check the website’s code for bugs but also visually inspect product pages to check that they render correctly.

summary.tldr:
Thinking Machines Labs Inc., founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has launched Inkling 2 Small, a large language model designed to automate AI training and research tasks. The company is reportedly seeking a $5 billion funding round led by Accel, which would value the firm at $40 billion. The model is currently available via the company's Tinker cloud service, with open-source weights scheduled for release next week.

Inkling 2 Small features 594 billion total parameters, with a 292-million-parameter vision encoder that enables visual verification of generated code and graphics. The model utilizes a dynamic compute architecture where approximately 17 billion parameters are activated per prompt, allowing users to adjust compute intensity for cost-efficiency. Training was conducted on GB300 NVL72 racks, requiring 68 hours for pre-training and nine days for reinforcement learning. The model was specifically honed on hundreds of thousands of "autoresearch" coding challenges, including kernel optimization and neural network post-training.

In performance testing, Inkling 2 Small reportedly doubled the forecasting score of the Qwen3.5-4B model in 4.5 hours. It also outperformed competitors such as Spark Open and Kimi K3 on various knowledge work and financial task benchmarks. The model supports user-led post-training for customization, with the company claiming faster learning rates compared to its previous iterations.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** Inkling 2 Small contains 594 billion total parameters, with a 292-million-parameter vision encoder and 17 billion active parameters per prompt.
**Training Infrastructure:** The model was trained on GB300 NVL72 racks, with a 68-hour pre-training phase followed by a nine-day reinforcement learning workflow.
**Performance Benchmark:** The model successfully fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B to double its weather forecasting score in 4.5 hours.
**Funding Context:** Thinking Machines is reportedly in talks for a $5 billion funding round led by Accel at a $40 billion valuation.
**Availability:** The model is accessible via the Tinker cloud service, with open-source weights expected to be released by mid-November 2026.

title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security.

The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It’s unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.

We regret to inform you…

Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It’s not clear why the company considered such information “non-sensitive.”

In a Wednesday update, the company said that part of the “ongoing multifront cyberattack” involved an “on-path attack” that exposed a subset of customer passwords, and that the attack vector had been identified and fixed. Also known as an adversary-in-the-middle attack, on-path attacks happen when a hacker gains access to a piece of infrastructure sending traffic back and forth between two parties. Chainalysis has yet to say where the infrastructure compromise occurred and if the data obtained from it was TLS encrypted.

The company said later that day that an investigation two days earlier (on Monday) had revealed that “certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor.” It also said it had detected “abnormal activity” and, in response, took down its login page and know-your-transaction service, which monitors threats to cryptocurrency holdings in real time. The company has also removed access to its Reactor and Data Solutions services.

In an update on Friday, Chainalysis said it had begun phasing in customer access to KYT and

summary.tldr:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis confirmed a significant security breach occurring in October, involving an 'on-path' (adversary-in-the-middle) attack that compromised sensitive data for its entire user base. The stolen information includes names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens. Affected clients include high-profile government entities such as the FBI, the US Air Force, and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, alongside private sector firms like Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays.

The breach was facilitated by AI agent-assisted offensive techniques, allowing unauthorized access to internal tools and infrastructure. Following the discovery of the full scope of the exposure on Monday, Chainalysis took its login page, Know-Your-Transaction (KYT) service, Reactor, and Data Solutions services offline. The company has since begun a phased restoration of services, requiring customers to provide trusted IP addresses for allow-listing and mandating a full credential reset for all users.

Despite the severity of the incident, Chainalysis maintains that there is no evidence that investigation data was accessed or that its attribution data was manipulated. The company has not disclosed the specific infrastructure point where the on-path attack occurred, whether the intercepted traffic was TLS-encrypted, or the specific mechanics of the AI agents utilized by the attackers. Chainalysis has declined to provide further comment beyond its official blog updates.
takeaways: **Compromised Data:** Attackers obtained names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens for all Chainalysis users.
**Attack Vector:** The breach utilized AI agent-assisted offensive techniques and an 'on-path' (adversary-in-the-middle) attack to intercept traffic.
**Service Impact:** Chainalysis suspended its login page, KYT, Address Screening, Reactor, and Data Solutions services in response to the incident.
**Remediation:** The company is implementing a mandatory credential rotation and requiring customers to submit trusted IP addresses for access restoration.

**Unanswered Questions:** The firm has not clarified why there was a two-day delay between discovering the full scope of the data theft and public disclosure, nor has it detailed the capabilities of the AI agents involved.

Tech companies, including OpenAI and Amazon, are facing mounting pressure to mitigate the impact of energy-intensive infrastructure on local power grids, water supplies, and air quality. **Regulatory Environment:** Despite reported moratoriums in states like Texas, permitting processes remain active, while federal lawmakers are considering legislation to accelerate energy projects despite calls for stricter environmental oversight.

title: AWS’ Colleen Aubrey: Stop inventing new AI metrics — it’s your business metrics that matter
author: Zeus Kerravala
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 13:56 EST / NOVEMBER 06 2026

AWS’ Colleen Aubrey: Stop inventing new AI metrics — it’s your business metrics that matter

There isn’t a business or information technology leader today who doesn’t have artificial intelligence at the top of their priority list. The challenge for most organizations is deciding what to measure and how to determine whether an AI initiative was successful.

To better understand how customers should approach AI metrics, I spoke with Colleen Aubrey from Amazon Web Services Inc ,, who has some deep experience in this area.

As senior vice president of Applied AI Solutions at AWS and a member of Amazon’s S-team, she builds on that foundation with lessons from 20-plus years at Amazon, where she built customer-facing products for millions of sellers and advertisers. The playbook she drew from that experience gives enterprises a practical path to move out of AI pilot purgatory, and it starts with throwing out the AI return-on-investment slide.

She argues that understanding AI ROI requires thinking in terms of business metrics. “I worry that people start trying to come up with new metrics to measure the impact of AI, but it’s the same metrics,” she explained. “It’s your business metrics that matter.” AWS has spent 20 years building cloud infrastructure. AI business applications are a much newer opportunity.

When Aubrey joined AWS, she inherited 35 application-layer programs. “I would say Connect for the contact center was probably our most successful example,” she told me in a recent interview ahead of AWS re:Invent Nov. 30-Dec. 4.

She studied what made it work: The team had deep operational experience running Amazon’s customer service function; it chose a sharp wedge (outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone rather than chasing feature parity; and the team knew its customers. The lessons from that success are now the blueprint for the expanded Amazon Connect family : Connect Customer, Connect Talent, Connect Health and Connect Decisions.

The playbook Aubrey built for the Connect family closely mirrors what IT leaders need to move their own AI programs out of pilot mode. Here are my five takeaways that should matter to IT leaders:

Feature parity is a trap

The first lesson Aubrey drew from her assessment was about where to start. Nobody runs a better supply chain than Amazon, which is exactly why the early version of AW

summary.tldr:
Colleen Aubrey, Senior Vice President of Applied AI Solutions at AWS, argues that enterprises must abandon specialized 'AI ROI' metrics—such as token counts or prompt volume—in favor of traditional business KPIs. Drawing on her experience managing 35 application-layer programs, including the Amazon Connect suite, Aubrey emphasizes that successful AI initiatives require a 'wedge' strategy: identifying a specific, high-pain decision point rather than attempting to replicate entire workflows or chasing feature parity with legacy vendors.

Technically, Aubrey highlights that AI often acts as a catalyst for exposing downstream operational inefficiencies rather than simply removing bottlenecks. For instance, Amazon’s internal deployment of coding assistants resulted in a twofold increase in production velocity only after the team addressed underlying issues in test coverage and pipeline health. She advocates for a 'humorphism' design philosophy, where AI interfaces are built to integrate into existing human workflows, and warns that shipping high-quality models with poor user experience will inevitably fail. Current AWS deployments, such as Connect Decisions, demonstrate this by scaling to 2,000 planners at Wells Vehicle Electronics, resulting in a 7% inventory reduction over three months.
takeaways: **Business Metric Alignment:** Projects must be tied to existing CFO-tracked metrics like working capital or cycle time; if a project cannot be measured against these, it remains an experiment rather than an investment.

**The Wedge Strategy:** Success in AI products like Amazon Connect came from focusing on a narrow, high-pain wedge (e.g., voice quality) rather than attempting to achieve feature parity with established ERP incumbents.

**Downstream Bottleneck Management:** AI deployment often exposes existing infrastructure weaknesses; Amazon achieved a 2x increase in production velocity by fixing test coverage and pipeline health rather than relying solely on coding assistants.

**Outcome-Based Roles:** Aubrey advises shifting job descriptions from task-based to outcome-based, noting that roles like 'UX tech' are emerging as AI automates traditional task-heavy responsibilities.
**Usability Philosophy:** AWS prioritizes 'humorphism,' designing AI to fit existing human work patterns, with a specific focus on closing the gap between internal prototypes and production-ready UX.

title: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web
author: Zack Whittaker
contentSnippet:
Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.

The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”

In a blog post , cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.

Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.

The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.

Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September . Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gam

summary.tldr:
Security researchers at Censys have identified over 800 instances of Artex—a Chinese-developed, open-source autonomous penetration testing tool—publicly exposed to the internet without password protection. Originally released in July, Artex functions as a system of AI agents capable of executing end-to-end cyberattacks, including reconnaissance and data exfiltration, with minimal human intervention. While intended for authorized security testing, the software's accessibility has enabled threat actors to leverage it for malicious operations, prompting the developers to transition the project to a closed-source model for paid customers only.

Microsoft and CrowdStrike have linked Artex to several high-profile cyberattacks, including a September campaign against the Korean finance industry and an October breach of IT support giant ConnectWise. In the latter, attackers utilized the tool to infiltrate cloud environments and exfiltrate data at speeds that hindered traditional defensive response times. Despite the shift to closed-source distribution, numerous copies of the Artex codebase remain available on public repositories, and the existing exposed instances continue to host sensitive attack data, including implants used for persistent network access.
takeaways: **Exposure Scale:** Censys identified more than 800 distinct, password-less deployments of Artex accessible via the public internet.
**Attack Capabilities:** Microsoft characterizes Artex as an autonomous agent system capable of performing the full cyberattack lifecycle, from initial reconnaissance to final data exfiltration.

**Documented Incidents:** The tool was used in a September attack against the Korean finance sector and an October breach of ConnectWise, which impacted thousands of organizations using Microsoft cloud services.
**Operational Vulnerabilities:** Many attacks involving Artex exploited basic security failures, specifically weak or known passwords and the absence of multi-factor authentication.
**Distribution Change:** Following widespread misuse, the Artex developers have moved the project to a closed-source, paid-access model, though legacy code remains available on public platforms.

title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet:
Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.

“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.

Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.

“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”

Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.

The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot , which were debuted with

summary.tldr:
Meta has introduced 'Spaces,' a new feature for its Muse AI agents designed to facilitate project-based collaboration. Spaces function as dedicated, persistent breakout conversations or 'custom experiences' accessible via the Muse interface sidebar. Users can initiate a Space by describing a goal—such as a wedding planner, holiday gift tracker, or DIY project board—which the Muse agent then constructs as a specialized project environment.

Technically, Spaces are designed to integrate with third-party applications, allowing the agent to pull external data and maintain real-time updates in the background. This enables the tracking of dynamic information like concert dates, price fluctuations, or savings progress without requiring manual user prompts. CEO Mark Zuckerberg noted the utility of these spaces for creating functional interfaces, citing personal examples including a BBQ game and a home control dashboard.

This launch follows the recent introduction of 'Muse Voice,' which enables verbal commands and video chat interactions with agents. Meta’s agent ecosystem, characterized by its 'cuddly' avatar design, reached 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada within two months of its debut, as reported during the company's October earnings call. Meta is positioning Muse within a competitive landscape of anthropomorphic AI agents, including OpenAI’s 'dots' and SpaceXAI’s 'Grokbot.'
takeaways: **Functional Scope:** Spaces act as persistent project boards or trackers that Muse agents build based on natural language descriptions.
**Third-Party Integration:** Spaces support background data synchronization with external apps to automatically update project information like pricing or scheduling.
**User Adoption:** Meta reported 10 million users for its Muse agents in the U.S. and Canada as of October, less than two months post-launch.
**Recent Feature Expansion:** Spaces is the second major Muse update in one week, following the release of Muse Voice for verbal and video-based interaction.

title: Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
author: Emma Roth
contentSnippet: Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within Muse. The new feature, called “spaces,” allows its AI assistant to build things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker, trivia game, and more, which you can interact with directly in the Muse app. Meta says you can create a new space by describing it. If you connect an outside app to Muse — like Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, Notion, and others Muse works with — the AI assistant will continuously pull information from them, allowing it to update pricing, dates, and other information in your space in the background. You can also interact with elements inside your spaces by checking things off, adding notes, and making edits. [Media: https://www.threads.com/@muse/post/DfaNbz4CMU8] You can also change the placement of your spaces in the Muse app, too, as Meta lets you keep them in the sidebar, move them into your main tab, or schedule when you see them. “For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday,” Meta says. Meta also announced that it’s bringing new “Active Memory” and “Active Focus” capabilities from its Muse Wonder AI model into the Muse app and its Meta AI chatbot. This will allow Muse to understand when past information becomes relevant during conversations, as well as make it better at working toward goals. Meta is rolling out spaces to all Muse users. The company is also looking into ways to share your spaces with other users and collaborate with them.

summary.tldr:
Meta has introduced 'Spaces' for its Muse AI application, a feature enabling users to generate custom, app-like interfaces through natural language prompts. These spaces function as specialized hubs—such as shopping dashboards, trivia games, or academic trackers—that integrate directly with third-party services including Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, and Notion. By connecting these external accounts, the AI performs background data synchronization, automatically updating pricing, scheduling, and task information within the user's custom interface.

Beyond creation, Meta has implemented granular UI controls, allowing users to pin spaces to a sidebar, move them to a main tab, or schedule their visibility based on the day of the week. Additionally, Meta is integrating 'Active Memory' and 'Active Focus' capabilities—derived from its Muse Wonder AI model—into both the Muse app and the broader Meta AI chatbot. These updates are designed to improve the model's contextual awareness of past interactions and its ability to execute multi-step goal-oriented tasks. The company is currently rolling out Spaces to all Muse users and is exploring future functionality for collaborative, shared spaces.
takeaways: **Integration Ecosystem:** Muse supports real-time data pulling from Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, and Notion to populate custom user dashboards.
**Model Upgrades:** The Muse app and Meta AI chatbot are incorporating 'Active Memory' and 'Active Focus' features from the Muse Wonder model to enhance contextual relevance and goal tracking.
**UI Customization:** Users can manage space visibility via sidebar pinning, main tab placement, and time-based scheduling.
**Deployment Status:** The Spaces feature is currently available to all Muse users, with collaborative sharing features under development.

title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
author: Shantanu Tripathi
contentSnippet: When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator. This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An ml.p4d.24xlarge has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach. Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation. This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did. One thing to know before you read further: GPU partitioning works on endpoints that use inference components , the construct you use to deploy several models to one endpoint and set the compute each model gets. Partitioning builds directly on it. A partition is a resource a component asks for, in the same place it already asks for CPU and memory. If you haven’t used inference components, this post introduces them. Single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, and heterogeneous instance pools cannot be partitioned. What customers do today, and why each option falls short If you have more models than accelerators, you have had three choices. Run fewer, larger endpoints and batch harder – This raises utilization, but only when the models are interchangeable. A portfolio of fine-tuned variants or per-tenant models is not. Use multi-model endpoints –  These load and unload models from a shared GPU on demand, which fits sparse, bursty traffic.

summary.tldr:
Amazon SageMaker Inference has introduced support for NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology, allowing users to partition a single physical GPU into multiple independent hardware-isolated instances. Previously, SageMaker required a minimum allocation of one full accelerator per model, which often led to underutilization on instances like the ml.p4d.24xlarge, where eight A100 GPUs could only host eight models regardless of individual memory requirements. By enabling hardware-enforced isolation of compute units and memory blocks, this update allows developers to deploy multiple models on a single GPU or select fractional GPU resources to better match specific model performance needs.

This feature is integrated directly into SageMaker's 'inference components' construct, which allows users to define compute and memory requirements for individual models within a single endpoint. The partitioning capability is specifically restricted to endpoints utilizing inference components; it is not supported for single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, or heterogeneous instance pools. This shift aims to resolve the previous trade-off between over-provisioning expensive hardware for small models and the latency overhead associated with loading and unloading models in multi-model endpoints.
takeaways: **Hardware Isolation:** NVIDIA MIG technology provides dedicated compute and memory blocks for each partition, enforced at the hardware level.
**Deployment Constraint:** GPU partitioning is exclusively available for endpoints using inference components and is incompatible with serverless or single-model endpoints.
**Resource Efficiency:** The update allows users to deploy more models than there are physical GPUs and select fractional GPU resources rather than full accelerators.
**Legacy Limitation:** Prior to this update, instances like the ml.p4d.24xlarge were limited to a maximum of eight models, regardless of whether the models required 14 GB or 40 GB of VRAM.

title: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick
author: Thomas Delteil
contentSnippet: Over the past year, as we built Amazon Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user. Take the user who says “ monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest ”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice. This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When? , What? , Who? , and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it. The framework at a glance Figure 1: How triggers, agents, and capabilities relate, with learning feeding back from the session runtime A trigger starts the work and carries the task ( When and What ), an agent takes it on ( Who ) and uses its capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) to perform the task ( How ). This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more. Triggers: What causes work to begin Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task. Human-initiated: A person opens a conversation and asks the agent to do something. Interactive, synchronous, conversational. Agent-delegated: One agent, mid-task, invokes another to handle a sub-problem. Programmatic, composable, potentially recursive. Scheduled: Time-based activation, like “run financial research every Monday at 9am.” Deterministic, with the same standing instructions applied across runs. Event-driven: A signal from an external system, such as a n

summary.tldr:
Amazon's internal development team for 'Amazon Quick' has formalized a taxonomy of agentic primitives to standardize the architecture of their agentic systems. The framework decomposes agentic work into four core questions—When, What, Who, and How—to resolve ambiguity in product design and system architecture. By establishing a shared vocabulary, the team aims to distinguish between triggers, agents, and capabilities, preventing the redundant development of similar functions under different nomenclature.

The taxonomy defines a 'Trigger' as the activation mechanism that addresses both the 'When' and 'What' of a task. Triggers are categorized into four types: Human-initiated (synchronous, conversational), Agent-delegated (programmatic, recursive sub-tasking), Scheduled (deterministic, time-based), and Event-driven (external system signals). An 'Agent' represents the 'Who' that executes the task, while 'Capabilities'—comprising tools, skills, and workflows—define the 'How.' The framework also incorporates a feedback loop where learning from session runtimes informs future agentic performance.
takeaways: **Taxonomy Framework:** Agentic work is decomposed into four primitives: Triggers (When/What), Agents (Who), and Capabilities (How).
**Trigger Classification:** Amazon Quick identifies four distinct trigger types: Human-initiated, Agent-delegated, Scheduled, and Event-driven.
**Capability Components:** The 'How' of the system is defined by three specific elements: tools, skills, and workflows.
**System Architecture:** The framework includes a feedback loop where learning from session runtimes is integrated back into the agentic operating system.

title: Zyphra ZYFA: FP8 FlashAttention for AMD MI355X, Up to 1.76x Faster
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Zyphra has released ZYFA (Zyphra FlashAttention on AMD) , a set of FP8 and BF16 prefill attention kernels for AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs. ZYFA is Zyphra’s FP8 attention engine for long-context prefill, and the code is open source under Apache 2.0 . On real model activations, its FP8 kernels run 1.16-1.76x faster than AITER , AMD’s default kernel library. At head dimension 128, ZYFA’s FP8 error is 62-78% lower than AITER’s. TL;DR Framework: It is a kernel library. Causal forward (prefill) attention in FP8 e4m3 and BF16, head dim 128 and MLA shape (192/128). Runs on: AMD Instinct MI355X only (CDNA4, gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, PyTorch 2.12. Drop-in flash_attn_func interface. Performance: 1.16-1.76x AITER’s FP8 throughput on real activations; BF16 roughly ties (1.01-1.02x). Best: 2,672 TFLOP/s FP8 at 32K tokens, 53% of the FP8 datasheet peak (AITER: 39%). Worst: Only 1.16x on Mistral-7B activations; FP8 clock drops to 1,628 MHz vs AITER’s 2,108 MHz. What is ZYFA? ZYFA is shipped in the form of a technical paper along with code from Zyphra. It powers the attention engine of the Zyphra Optimization Engine (ZOE) , which runs Zyphra Cloud. The BF16 kernels are written in HIP. The FP8 kernels are hand-scheduled assembly emitted by a Python generator. Why does FP8 attention underperform on MI355X? FP8 matrix instructions run at 2x the BF16 peak. But FP8 only speeds up the 2 matrix products, QKᵀ and PV. The softmax between them runs on the vector unit at the same speed in both precisions. For 32 queries against 128 keys, FP8 matrix work takes 1,024 cycles. The exact FP8 softmax takes 896 vector cycles. So the kernel needs near-perfect overlap to keep matrix units busy. Zyphra’s thread traces show AITER’s matrix pipe idle for 31.7% of cycles. The MI355X does not track matrix instruction completion in hardware, so instruction order must create that overlap. How does ZYFA work? ZYFA uses 3 techniques : Lean P: one multiply-add instead of an exponential An e4m3 bit pattern, read as an integer, grows by 8 each time the value doubles. So the code of 2^x is roughly 8x plus a constant. Lean P writes each FP8 probability with 1 multiply-add and 1 integer conversion. This cuts softmax vector cycles per block from 896 to 384. Two-wave ping-pong schedule 2 waves share each SIMD. One issues matrix instructions while the other computes probabilities, then they swap. With lean P, the matrix

summary.tldr:
Zyphra has released ZYFA (Zyphra FlashAttention on AMD), an open-source (Apache 2.0) kernel library designed to optimize long-context prefill attention for AMD Instinct MI355X (CDNA4, gfx950) GPUs. The library provides drop-in compatibility with the flash_attn_func interface and supports FP8 (e4m3) and BF16 precisions, specifically targeting head dimensions of 128 and MLA shapes (192/128). ZYFA is built on ROCm 7.2.3 and PyTorch 2.12, serving as the attention engine for the Zyphra Optimization Engine (ZOE) used in Zyphra Cloud.

Technically, ZYFA addresses the bottleneck where FP8 matrix instructions (QKᵀ and PV) are limited by the vector-unit-bound softmax operation. By implementing 'Lean P'—a technique that approximates the exponential function using a single multiply-add and integer conversion—Zyphra reduces softmax vector cycles per block from 896 to 384. Combined with a two-wave ping-pong scheduling strategy that overlaps matrix instruction issuance with probability computation, ZYFA achieves 1.16-1.76x the throughput of AMD’s default AITER library on real model activations. At 32K tokens, ZYFA reaches 2,672 TFLOP/s (53% of FP8 datasheet peak), compared to AITER’s 39%.
takeaways: **Performance Gains:** ZYFA delivers 1.16-1.76x higher FP8 throughput than AITER, with BF16 performance remaining roughly equivalent (1.01-1.02x).
**Accuracy Improvement:** At head dimension 128, ZYFA reduces FP8 error by 62-78% compared to the AITER library.
**Optimization Techniques:** The library utilizes 'Lean P' to replace standard exponential calculations with a single multiply-add and integer conversion, significantly reducing vector unit overhead.
**Scheduling Strategy:** ZYFA employs a two-wave ping-pong schedule to maximize matrix pipe utilization, addressing the lack of hardware-level matrix instruction completion tracking on the MI355X.
**Implementation Details:** BF16 kernels are written in HIP, while FP8 kernels utilize hand-scheduled assembly generated via a Python-based emitter.

title: After the midterms, is the AI industry in for a rough two years?
author: Theresa Loconsolo, Anthony Ha

Democrats’ historic victories in this week’s U.S. midterm elections could also transform the tech industry.

title: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate
author: Aishwarya Pawar
contentSnippet: Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application. Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between. Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control. As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi-day engineering effort. Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow. To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to address this problem for planning teams in NASC. The server acts as a centralized, agent-agnostic gateway between AI agents and our enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON metadata file that the server discovers automatically on the next pipeline sync. In this post, we describe the architecture, show how a metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and explain how the serverless infrastructure supports multiple agents and applications in a multi-tenant environment. Problem statement and design goals Two interrelated challenges shaped how we designed this system: fragmented data access patterns and an unsustainable onboarding model. Integration challenge at scale Our data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain-specific data. Multiple teams wanted AI assistants that could query this data conversationally, but each built its own integration from scratch. Each agent embedded its own SQL generation logic, schema knowledge, and connection handling, so a schema change meant patching every agent individually. Access control was fragmented, with no single audit point for data access decisions. Onboarding a new dataset required custom tool code, query validation, and redeployment, typically a multi-day effort per table. Design goals We established four requirements: Configuration-driven data la

summary.tldr:
Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) engineering team has developed a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server deployed on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate to centralize AI agent access to enterprise data lakes. The architecture serves as an agent-agnostic gateway, decoupling LLM agents from direct database and API integrations. This design addresses the operational bottleneck of fragmented data access, where previously each agent required custom SQL generation logic, schema management, and connection handling, leading to inconsistent permission enforcement and high maintenance overhead.

The system utilizes a metadata-driven approach to streamline data onboarding. By defining new datasets via JSON metadata files, the server automatically discovers and exposes data during pipeline synchronization, eliminating the need for per-dataset custom code or redeployments. This centralized gateway architecture allows for unified audit logging and consistent access control enforcement across multiple agents and applications. The serverless infrastructure is designed to scale in a multi-tenant environment, supporting the NASC network's requirement for conversational access to thousands of operational, business, and domain-specific datasets.
takeaways: **Architecture:** Serverless MCP server hosted on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate.
**Onboarding Mechanism:** Metadata-driven discovery using JSON files, removing the need for custom integration code per dataset.
**Problem Addressed:** Eliminates fragmented data access patterns and redundant SQL generation logic across multiple AI agents.
**Operational Scope:** Supports thousands of datasets within the Amazon North America Sort Center (NASC) data lake.
