title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2
author: Hammad Ausaf
contentSnippet: In Part 1 , you built a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server. The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Three things that are fine for one agent and two tools become the work in an enterprise with hundreds of agents and thousands of tools: What Part 1 does Why it stops scaling What Part 2 does instead The agent holds each MCP server’s runtime ARN and calls it directly N agents against M servers is a wiring matrix, and every new tool touches every agent that needs it Agents reach one Gateway endpoint, and the Gateway holds the target registry The agent’s role holds the token-exchange permission and reads the provider’s secret Every agent that acts for users gets a credential path to every resource it might reach The Gateway redeems the grant, and the agent’s role holds no token-exchange or secret permissions Each MCP server carries the same groups check in its own code The same rule, copied into thousands of servers, drifts and can’t be audited or changed in one place One default-deny Cedar policy set, evaluated at the Gateway before tools run In this post, you make that change on the Part 1 solution. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applicati

summary.tldr:
Amazon Web Services has detailed the second phase of its Amazon Bedrock AgentCore architecture, focusing on scaling governance for AI agents using Okta Cross App Access (XAA). While the initial implementation relied on a direct wiring matrix where agents held individual runtime ARNs and tool-specific authorization logic, the updated architecture introduces the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. This gateway acts as a centralized front door, decoupling agents from tool registries and consolidating authorization checks into a single point of entry.

The new framework replaces distributed, redundant authorization code within Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers with a centralized Cedar policy set. By evaluating these policies at the Gateway, the system ensures that agents only access tools within the scope delegated by Okta, eliminating the need for agents to hold individual token-exchange permissions or provider secrets. The architecture supports multi-environment deployment, demonstrated by adding a second agent running on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) that authenticates via its own Okta identity. Observability is managed through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability integrated with Amazon CloudWatch, providing a unified audit trail for all access decisions.
takeaways: **Architecture Shift:** Transitioned from a direct N-to-M agent-to-tool wiring matrix to a centralized Gateway-based topology.
**Policy Engine:** Replaced per-server authorization code with a default-deny Cedar policy set evaluated at the Gateway.
**Credential Management:** Removed token-exchange and secret permissions from individual agent roles, centralizing grant redemption at the Gateway.
**Multi-Environment Support:** Validated the Gateway architecture by deploying a secondary agent on Amazon EKS with a distinct Okta identity.
**Observability:** Centralized audit logging for all access decisions using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability and Amazon CloudWatch.

title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
author: Hammad Ausaf
contentSnippet: An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end. In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch. Solution overview Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime. Figure 1: Solu

summary.tldr:
Okta and Amazon Web Services have introduced a governance framework for AI agents using Okta Cross App Access (XAA) and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture positions Okta as the governance plane, where administrators register agents and define application access policies, while Amazon Bedrock AgentCore serves as the execution plane. This integration ensures that agent actions are evaluated against identity policies in real-time, preventing unauthorized access that traditional OAuth consent or shared service accounts might overlook.

The technical implementation utilizes two specific Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities: AgentCore Runtime, which validates Okta grants, and AgentCore Identity, which exchanges those grants for short-lived access tokens stored in a secure vault. This process abstracts credentials away from the agent code itself. Performance testing indicates that the AgentCore Identity layer adds approximately 0.6 seconds to a 30-second end-to-end request. Furthermore, security enforcement is highly responsive; Okta revokes agent requests for a user within approximately 1 second of assignment removal, with existing tokens expiring within 5 minutes.
takeaways: **Governance Architecture:** Okta acts as the central policy engine, while Amazon Bedrock AgentCore handles credential management and token exchange via its Runtime and Identity capabilities.
**Latency Impact:** Integrating AgentCore Identity adds roughly 0.6 seconds of overhead to a standard 30-second agent request cycle.
**Revocation Speed:** Okta policy enforcement is near-instant, with new agent requests blocked within 1 second of user assignment removal and existing tokens expiring within 5 minutes.
**Credential Security:** The AgentCore Identity vault ensures that agent code never directly handles or sees the underlying access credentials.

title: AI is the new dating dealbreaker
author: Helen Li
contentSnippet: When Irene moved to San Francisco last year, she started using dating apps as a way to meet new people, get to know her new city, and connect with others who care about the things she does. After the 25-year-old analyst downloaded Hinge and started swiping, she noticed a trend. “Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if”,” she recalls. “Sometimes people will be like, ‘Fuck AI.’” Usually, the people who include this kind of value statement on their profile work in the arts, nursing, maybe graphic design. Within the span of a few minutes of sitting down and swiping, Irene shows me a second profile where this happened once more: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.” In San Francisco, the epicenter of tech, the metaphorical AI bomb went off in 2022 with the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Conversations surrounding artificial intelligence now permeate the dating scene in one shape or another. Over the past month, I bopped around the city —, chatting with people at parties and coworking spaces and reviewing dating directories and other online profiles —, trying to find out how AI affects the dating scene. Responses varied wildly. For some, AI feelings take on a similar valence to traditionally political ones, showing up in dating profiles next to party affiliation or other signifiers, like the watermelon emoji symbolizing solidarity with Palestinians amid the war in Gaza. Others are wrestling with the ethics of dating someone who builds AI, considering the financial benefits a partner in the industry can bring, weighing whether to have children in a future this uncertain, or even handing their love lives over to it entirely. On a street near Berkeley, I meet up with Kyle. (His name has been changed so that he can talk openly about his personal life.) Kyle is a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit initiative, and although he is just in his early 20s, he’s already thinking about death. In the AI safety community, some experts see a 10 percent chance of humans going extinct due to AI taking over. This apocalyptic possibility is always top of mind when he navigates conversations with a potential partner: The rapid development of AI shapes how he thinks about whether he wants to have kids or where he might live long term — if there is even a long term. “A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years d

summary.tldr:
Artificial intelligence has emerged as a polarizing social and political signifier within the San Francisco dating scene, with users increasingly listing anti-AI sentiments as dealbreakers on platforms like Hinge. While some individuals view AI development as an existential threat—citing the 10% extinction risk often discussed in AI safety circles—others view the industry as a source of significant financial stability. This divide is underscored by the economic reality of the Bay Area, where over 20,000 AI-related jobs were added in the last year, and AI researcher salaries frequently reach $300,000, leading matchmakers to report increased client interest in partners employed by firms approaching IPOs, such as Anthropic and OpenAI.

Beyond social signaling, AI is fundamentally altering the mechanics of modern courtship. A 2025 survey by Match and the Kinsey Institute indicates that 26% of U.S. singles now utilize AI tools to enhance their dating experiences. Practical applications range from using chatbots for emotional regulation to the deployment of automated AI agents that handle swiping, messaging, and calendar scheduling for busy founders. Despite these efficiencies, the trend raises concerns regarding the erosion of human connection, with 38% of Americans reporting they disclose personal information to chatbots that they would withhold from their own romantic partners.
takeaways: **Economic Impact:** The San Francisco Bay Area added over 20,000 AI jobs in the past year, even as the broader tech sector contracted by 6% since 2022.

**Usage Statistics:** A 2025 Match/Kinsey Institute survey found 26% of U.S. singles use AI tools for dating, while 38% of Americans report sharing personal secrets with chatbots rather than human partners.

**Automated Dating:** Some users are deploying custom AI agents—built using tools like Claude Code—to automate Hinge swiping and conversation, with one founder reporting an average of two in-person dates per week via this method.
**Platform Integration:** Hinge has introduced AI-generated response suggestions, and Bumble is transitioning its core interface away from traditional swiping toward AI-facilitated matchmaking.
**Compensation Benchmarks:** AI researcher roles in the current market are commanding average salaries of approximately $300,000.

title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Greenlight Financial has deployed an autonomous Security Operations Center (SOC) solution named Luna, built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to manage between 3,000 and 4,000 security and risk alerts monthly. By utilizing AgentCore runtime for hosting agent code and AgentCore memory for state management, the company has automated the resolution of over 90% of these alerts without human intervention. The system is designed to handle sensitive financial data while adhering to the regulatory standards required of major banking institutions.

Luna utilizes a multi-tiered supervisor architecture comprising more than 30 specialized agents that perform triage across four primary vectors: dark web breach-card alerts, identity and access anomalies, infrastructure alerts from EDR/SIEM/observability tools, and financial risk events such as suspicious transaction patterns. The system employs episodic memory to facilitate continuous learning, allowing it to cross-reference data sources—such as card activity status, deduplication, customer session history, and open support tickets—in seconds, a process that previously required manual analyst review.
takeaways: **Automation Scale:** Luna resolves over 90% of 3,000–4,000 monthly security and risk alerts without human intervention.
**Architecture:** The system uses a multi-tiered supervisor model with over 30 specialized agents hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
**Data Vectors:** Triage covers dark web breach cards, identity/access anomalies, infrastructure alerts (EDR/SIEM), and financial risk/fraud indicators.
**Infrastructure Components:** Greenlight leverages AgentCore runtime for agent execution and AgentCore memory to support the multi-agent system's state and learning.

title: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Karan Nayak
contentSnippet: Taxbit is a digital-asset tax and accounting compliance platform. Founded in 2018, Taxbit helps enterprises such as exchanges, payment services, and brokers calculate gains and losses, collect tax documentation, and file information returns at scale. Now, a cited, permission-aware AI assistant helps compliance teams find answers right inside the product dashboard. But the knowledge needed to use that dashboard well was scattered across the public website, API documentation, and help-center articles, and a meaningful share was never written down at all. When a customer asked “what does this form status mean?”, they either went digging or filed a support ticket. Today more than 55 percent of users who ask Assist a question return to ask another within 24 hours, according to Taxbit’s internal production analytics. In this post, we share how we built Taxbit Assist , the AI assistant now embedded in the Taxbit dashboard, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. We cover the architecture, the retrieval work that made answers trustworthy enough to ship to regulated customers, how we handle safety and data residency, and how we continuously measure answer quality on live production traffic. What the assistant had to get right A generic chatbot was not an option in this domain. Four constraints shaped what we built: Grounded and cited – Our users make filing decisions. Every answer had to trace back to a source the user could open and read, and when the assistant didn’t know something, it had to say so. Role and organization awareness – The assistant shouldn’t walk a Support User through an admin-only workflow and send them to a page that they can’t open. summary.tldr:
Taxbit, a digital-asset tax and accounting compliance platform founded in 2018, has launched 'Taxbit Assist,' an AI-powered assistant integrated directly into its product dashboard. Built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the tool is designed to provide compliance teams with immediate, cited answers to product-related queries, reducing the need for manual documentation searches or support tickets. Internal production analytics indicate that over 55 percent of users who interact with the assistant return to ask a follow-up question within 24 hours.

The architecture prioritizes accuracy and regulatory compliance, adhering to four core constraints: providing grounded, cited responses linked to source documentation; enforcing role-based access control to prevent unauthorized workflow guidance; strictly distinguishing between product documentation and prohibited tax advice; and ensuring regional data residency. Taxbit operates the assistant under its existing compliance framework, which includes ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management), ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, and SOC 2 Type II certification. The company explicitly states that it does not train or fine-tune models using customer data.
takeaways: **Platform Foundation:** Taxbit Assist is built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a framework for scaling and optimizing AI agents.
**User Engagement:** Internal metrics show a 55% repeat-usage rate within 24 hours for users who engage with the assistant.
**Compliance Standards:** The system is developed in alignment with ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, and SOC 2 Type II reporting.
**Data Privacy:** Taxbit maintains a policy of not training or fine-tuning models on customer data to ensure security and regulatory adherence.

title: Big Tech lost big in the 2026 election
author: David Pierce
contentSnippet: On Tuesday, millions of American voters went to the polls and voted overwhelmingly for Democrats and against AI. The fight against Big Tech is about to come roaring back, and the fight over data centers is looking even harder for the folks trying to build them. On this episode of The Vergecast, Nilay and David discuss what the 2026 midterms mean for the tech industry going forward. They dig into the self-quarantining echo chamber that is X, the congressional energy likely to be pointed at tech CEOs and AI regulation, and whether anything is actually likely to get done in the next two years. After that, the hosts turn to AI. Specifically, whether anyone has figured out how to make money on AI. Specifically, whether OpenAI’s explosive growth in web search means much, when even Google can’t figure out how to make money on AI web search. Businesses are scaling back; agents don’t appear to be taking over. There’s a lot of money flowing around the AI world, but is there enough flowing into it to keep everything going? That’s the hard part. Finally, it’s time for a somewhat abridged Brendan Carr Is a Dummy, the latest on SpaceX’s mobile ambitions, the touchscreen MacBook, RAM Altman, and much more. Watch | Listen | Get ad-free In case you missed it this week: We also talked about the challenges of cloud gaming, the data center election, Rian Johnson’s new iPhone app, and the future of reading. And we want to hear all your thoughts about all of it! Call the Vergecast Hotline at 866-VERGE11, send us an email at vergecast@theverge.com, and tell us everything that’s on your mind. And make sure you subscribe so you don’t miss an episode!

summary.tldr:
The 2026 U.S. midterm elections resulted in a significant electoral shift toward Democratic candidates, signaling a potential increase in regulatory scrutiny and legislative pressure on the technology sector. The Vergecast hosts Nilay Patel and David Pierce analyze the implications for Big Tech, specifically highlighting the growing political resistance to AI development and the increasing difficulty of securing infrastructure approvals for new data centers. The discussion posits that the next two years of congressional activity will likely focus on aggressive oversight of tech CEOs and AI-related policy.

Beyond the political landscape, the episode examines the commercial viability of AI, questioning whether current business models can sustain the massive capital expenditures required for the industry. The hosts contrast OpenAI’s expansion into web search with Google’s ongoing struggle to monetize AI-integrated search results. They note a broader trend of businesses scaling back AI investments, observing that autonomous AI agents have not yet achieved widespread adoption or utility, raising concerns about the long-term financial sustainability of the current AI investment cycle.
takeaways: **Political Climate:** The 2026 midterms saw voters favor Democratic candidates, creating a challenging environment for Big Tech and data center expansion projects.
**Monetization Challenges:** Industry leaders, including Google and OpenAI, face significant hurdles in generating profitable revenue streams from AI-powered web search.
**Market Sentiment:** Businesses are reportedly scaling back AI initiatives as the anticipated transition to autonomous AI agents has failed to materialize at scale.
**Regulatory Outlook:** The upcoming two-year legislative cycle is expected to feature heightened congressional focus on AI regulation and the activities of major technology executives.

title: How Akai and Moog are embracing vibe-coded mods
author: Terrence O’Brien
contentSnippet: inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more, has decided to embrace the modding community. In an interview with The Verge, inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell said, “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want.” That “toolbox” includes making the code for devices like the recently teased MPC Sample Key open source, but also offering developers an SDK to make modifications easier and lessen the risk of bricking your beloved sampler. While Akai is eager to see what the modding community cooks up, and has started seeding devices to developers ahead of the official release of the Sample Key, the company takes reliability seriously. O’Donnell said the company wants to “make sure that our official software is completely stable and good for an artist on stage.” He can’t have Fred Again going on stage and discovering his MPC is riddled with bugs. But he also wants people to feel comfortable tinkering. “We’ll try to give them a reset button,” he said so “They can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.” The company is planning to make a big splash NAMM, the annual convention of music manufacturers in Anaheim, with Creator Lab, where it will let technically curious musicians get some hands-on time hacking 22 new products from across its brands. That includes products from Moog, that might not seem like a natural pairing for vibe coding because of its analog design. But O’Donnell thinks it can be, “if we open it up correctly.” That will involve building a platform for devs to work around the analog parts of the circuit. Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine, Polyend open-sourced its line of Tracker grooveboxes, and Behringer has also announced a slew of open-source devices, including a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller. The change in the industry has been quick and seismic. O’Donnell said of the need to provide developers tools for hacking inMusic’s products, “I can tell you it wasn’t on our task list five weeks ago. It just all of a sudden has to be on a task list now.” Of course, not everyone is thrilled. Elektron ha

summary.tldr:
inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, and Native Instruments, is pivoting to support the hardware modding community by providing official SDKs and open-source code for its devices. CEO Jack O’Donnell announced that the company will release the source code for upcoming products like the MPC Sample Key and provide a 'toolbox' to facilitate modifications while minimizing the risk of bricking hardware. To ensure stability for professional use, inMusic plans to implement a 'reset button' feature, allowing users to experiment with custom firmware without permanently compromising the device's core functionality.

The company intends to showcase this initiative at the upcoming NAMM convention in Anaheim through its 'Creator Lab,' where attendees can hack 22 new products across its brands, including analog Moog synthesizers. This shift follows a broader industry trend toward open-source hardware, with competitors like Erica Synths, Polyend, and Behringer—the latter of which recently announced a $150 MPC One clone named Kick—already releasing source code or open-source devices. While inMusic views this as a necessary evolution, other manufacturers like Elektron remain cautious, explicitly banning links to modified firmware on their official forums due to concerns regarding warranty voiding and hardware damage.
takeaways: **inMusic Strategy:** The company is developing an SDK and open-source code for devices like the MPC Sample Key to encourage community modding while maintaining a 'reset' safety feature.

**Industry Competitors:** Behringer has announced several open-source products, including the $150 'Kick' (MPC One clone), an E-mu SP-1200 clone, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61.
**Elektron Stance:** Elektron prohibits links to modified firmware on its official forums, citing risks to warranty coverage, future update compatibility, and the potential for bricking devices.
**NAMM Creator Lab:** inMusic will provide hands-on access to 22 new products for hacking at the Anaheim NAMM convention, including efforts to open up analog Moog circuits for developer modification.

title: How NVIDIA Open Source Tools Are Helping Researchers Build Next-Generation 6G Networks
author: Soma Velayutham
contentSnippet: A year ago, NVIDIA open sourced its Aerial wireless software , joining Sionna and a broader suite of open source tools for accelerating next-generation 6G network development. Together, they give researchers a foundation for testing ideas, comparing results and building on each other’s work — connecting simulation and AI training with experiments on real over-the-air wireless systems. Today, researchers and developers are using these tools to build 6G-ready networks that do more than just transmit data — receiving signals more effectively, keeping robots and autonomous systems connected when it matters most, and adapting in real time as devices move through the world. Over the past year, global developer adoption of NVIDIA AI Aerial and NVIDIA Sionna software has grown 10x, while NVIDIA’s open source 5G/6G tools have surpassed 1 million downloads. More than 8,000 research and academic institutions worldwide are using these platforms. The projects emerging today offer a view of how future networks could look. Each addresses a different challenge, but together point toward a broader ambition for building AI-native 6G networks that deliver connectivity, computing and sensing over a converged software-defined platform for billions of people, machines and agents. Networks That Help Robots React Faster A robot picking up an object needs to understand its surroundings and act before they change. When the AI powering that decision runs on a nearby server or in the cloud, the wireless connection becomes part of the response time. Researchers are exploring a more efficient approach called goal-oriented semantic communications. Instead of sending full images, robots transmit compact descriptions of objects, their positions and their relationships. Transmitting just as much information as needed allows robots to more quickly respond, especially in dynamic environments like workplaces and warehouses. At King’s College London , researchers connected a camera-equipped robot arm to an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin running NVIDIA Sionna, which supports both software-defined 5G network and edge AI processing. In fruit-packing and cube-stacking experiments with deliberately introduced faults, the approach reduced robot task completion time by up to 52.6% and improved task success compared with sending periodic images. NVIDIA has reported a 10x growth in developer adoption for its AI Aerial and Sionna software suites over the past year, with total downloads for its 5G/6G open-source toolkits exceeding 1 million. These platforms are currently utilized by over 8,000 academic and research institutions to develop AI-native 6G networks that integrate connectivity, computing, and sensing into a single software-defined architecture. The primary objective is to transition from traditional data transmission to intelligent, goal-oriented semantic communications capable of supporting autonomous systems and robotics.

Technical implementation focuses on reducing latency in robotic decision-making by replacing full-image transmission with compact, semantic descriptions of environmental objects and spatial relationships. In a specific deployment at King’s College London, researchers integrated a camera-equipped robot arm with an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin running Sionna. **Performance Benchmark:** Researchers at King’s College London demonstrated a 52.6% reduction in robot task completion time using goal-oriented semantic communications on a Jetson AGX Orin.
**Core Technology:** The Sionna software supports software-defined 5G networking and edge AI processing, enabling real-time adaptation for autonomous systems.

title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO
author: Rebecca Bellan
contentSnippet:
Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it.

A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.

As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.

“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”

Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.

Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.

“If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.”

“The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.

October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.

Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace.

summary.tldr: Data from financial platform Ramp indicates that corporate AI spending has stalled despite rising token volumes, challenging the assumption of continued hypergrowth for major model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic. While token spend grew 42% month-over-month in July, that growth plummeted to just 1.5% across August and September. Ramp’s lead economist, Ara Kharazian, attributes this stagnation to a combination of aggressive price competition, increased customer efficiency, and a saturation of high-intensity usage among the top 1% of "AI-pilled" firms, which had previously peaked at $10,000 in monthly spend per employee.
takeaways: **Spending Deceleration:** Token spend growth dropped from 42% in July to 1.5% in August and September, with a slight re-acceleration of 8.9% observed between September 23 and October 23.

**Price War Impact:** OpenAI and Anthropic have significantly reduced API pricing—including cuts for GPT-6 Sol/Luna and Fable 5.1/Opus 5.5—with Anthropic noting these reductions slashed revenue growth by approximately $600 million.

**Efficiency Gains:** Enterprises are increasingly using model routers and budget controls to shift workloads from expensive models to cheaper, lightweight alternatives, effectively decoupling token volume from revenue growth.

**Valuation Adjustments:** Amidst these headwinds, Anthropic’s estimated valuation reportedly fell from $2 trillion to $1.2–$1.3 trillion, while OpenAI lowered its valuation target from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion and reduced fundraising goals by $10 billion.

**Market Segmentation:** While top-tier firms spend $600–$1,000 per employee monthly, median firms spend only $12–$15, suggesting that the "hypergrowth" model may not scale to broader, less technical industries like healthcare or retail.

title: Midterm elections will put AI and data centers on trial, but Big Tech may end up winning anyway
author: Robert Hof
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 10:09 EST / NOVEMBER 06 2026

Midterm elections will put AI and data centers on trial, but Big Tech may end up winning anyway

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

It may be a little soon to determine the ultimate winners and losers among enterprise suppliers after the midterm elections, but the early line is: Big Tech wins and data center suppliers operators such as chipmakers and neoclouds lose. Or will everybody lose?

The day after the elections, stocks of many tech companies shot up, a bit paradoxically because investors apparently believe potential limits on AI and data centers could tamp down spending on compute and thus improve tech company margins that have made investors nervous. But then on Thursday, tech stocks almost across the board plunged back down even more for a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap — the Nasdaq fell more than 5.5% — on more generalized worries that, well, the AI boom could slow. Suffice to say, investors are still sorting things out.

Marvell Semiconductor this week made a surprisingly huge acquisition with Lumentum, a bet on the AI boom continuing. That is, if it comes off: The drop in Lumentum’s stock price has some speculating it could hunt around for another offer .

And the AI juggernaut indeed continues apace, judging from strong tech earnings, though even pre-election, they reflected investor wariness. AMD, Supermicro and Arista all beat easily, as well as Palantir and Kyndryl, whose stock rocketed 30%. But chipmakers Qualcomm, Arm and Globalfoundries didn’t get the love despite good quarters — especially in Thursday’s bloodbath.

All of which raises the question that Dave Vellante posed in his Breaking Analysis last weekend: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Dave and analyst Crawford Del Prete discussed the prospects.

Next week’s earnings reports include Cisco, CoreWeave, Applied Materials, Cerebras and Nebius, any or all of which could move markets.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

Analysis, opinion and food for thought

Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep No, data centers won’t get shut down, and AI will continue apace — just regulated as it needs to be, and we can hope it’s in the right way to protect people and communities and innovation all at the same time.

summary.tldr:
Following the 2026 midterm elections, tech markets experienced extreme volatility, with a $2.5 trillion collective market cap loss and a 5.5% drop in the Nasdaq on November 6. Despite investor anxiety regarding potential AI and data center regulation, major enterprise players continue to report strong earnings, including AMD, Supermicro, Arista, and Palantir. The industry is currently defined by massive M&A activity, most notably Marvell Semiconductor’s $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum and OpenAI’s reported $11 billion funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation.

Technical and commercial momentum remains focused on agentic AI and infrastructure scaling. OpenAI has introduced 'GPT-6 Cyber' for vulnerability research, while startups like fal ($16B valuation) and Traversal ($1B valuation) continue to secure significant capital. Enterprise software providers are pivoting toward agent-centric architectures, with Salesforce acquiring Cresta for $2.7 billion and Meta acquiring coding startup Conductor. Meanwhile, hardware and cloud infrastructure providers are navigating a shift where enterprises are hitting GPU utilization ceilings, forcing a move toward more efficient cloud storage and private cloud deployments.
takeaways: **Major M&A:** Marvell Semiconductor is acquiring Lumentum for $115 billion; Salesforce is acquiring Cresta for $2.7 billion; CrowdStrike is acquiring Fiddler AI and Dreadnode for $495 million.
**OpenAI Financials:** OpenAI reportedly raised $11 billion in new funding, reaching a $1.25 trillion valuation, and is acquiring developer tooling startup Pierre Computer.
**Market Performance:** Kyndryl shares surged 30% on hyperscaler growth, while Atlassian shares fell 17% due to subscription growth forecasts; Cloudflare revenue growth accelerated to 39%.

**New AI Models:** OpenAI launched GPT-6 Cyber for vulnerability research; Tencent released Hy4, a frontier model with visual understanding and computer use capabilities; Cogent Security debuted the VR-1.1 model for vulnerability repair.
**Startup Funding:** Generative media startup fal raised $1.3 billion at a $16 billion valuation; Traversal raised $120 million at a $1 billion valuation; 42AI launched with $62.5 million.

contentSnippet: Members of the action group Geef Tegengas put a banner on a crane during a protest. | Image: Getty Images Protesters have broken into a construction site of a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam this morning. Members of the Geef Tegengas group helped organize the protest against the construction of three 85-meter data center towers in the outskirts of Amsterdam. Reuters reports that around 100 people made it into the construction site, with some scaling a crane to place a "fuck AI" banner. Protesters also unfurled a "Microsoft powers genocide" banner on the construction site, and chanted "Microsoft has got to go" and "free Palestine." title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
author: Grace Huckins
contentSnippet: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour. I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round. Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.  But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors. With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. summary.tldr:
San Francisco-based startup Tau Robotics is currently deploying humanoid robots for residential cleaning services, utilizing a teleoperation model to gather training data for future autonomous capabilities. The robots, which stand four-and-a-half feet tall, are remotely piloted by human operators who view live feeds from cameras mounted in the robot's head and wrists. This data collection loop is designed to train models for independent task execution, focusing on household chores like folding laundry and wiping surfaces.

Technically, the robots feature 3D-printed heads equipped with antennae for communication with Tau headquarters and 3D-printed claw-style end effectors, which the company prefers over more complex human-like hands due to superior durability. The units are outfitted with protective grippy socks to prevent floor damage. While the robots are physically capable of performing tasks, they currently rely on human kinematic guidance for complex movements, functioning more like sophisticated radio-controlled devices than fully autonomous agents. Pricing has evolved from an initial $30 per hour for a single robot to a current structure of $60 for a weekly visit with two robots or $100 for a single one-time session.
takeaways: **Robot Specifications:** The units are 4.5 feet tall, utilize 3D-printed claw hands, and feature head-mounted and wrist-mounted cameras for remote pilot visibility.
**Operational Model:** The robots are currently teleoperated by humans rather than autonomous, with the primary business objective being the collection of kinematic data for future model training.
**Pricing Structure:** Current service rates are $60 for a weekly cleaning session involving two robots, or $100 for a single one-time visit.

**Technical Limitations:** The robots require human kinematic guidance for tasks such as folding laundry and making beds, and are described as being thorough but significantly slower than manual cleaning.
