title: Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M
author: Marina Temkin
contentSnippet:
Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.

Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source. The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.

Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment. The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.

The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily. Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from DataDog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week.

If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.

In September, Palo Alto Networks acquired Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks. The transaction valued Console at $500 million in stock and cash, TechCrunch reported. Other VC-backed companies that Palo Alto Networks has scooped up this year include NEA-backed Embrace, for $325 million ; Chronosphere, an observability platform backed by Greylock and Lux Capital, for $2.95 billion ; and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $231 million , according to regulatory filings.

Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired. Cyera, a cybersecurity startup valued at $12 billion earlier this year, acquired Oasis Security, which, like Clutch, focuses on managing AI agents’ access to systems, for $1 billion . Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.

Topics AI , Lightspeed Venture Capital , M&A , palo alto networks , Security , signalfire When you pur

summary.tldr:
Palo Alto Networks is currently in negotiations to acquire Clutch Security, a three-year-old startup specializing in securing AI agent access to enterprise systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based incentives. The deal, if finalized, would represent a significant valuation premium, as Clutch is currently generating approximately $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR), placing the acquisition multiple at roughly 50x ARR. This follows Clutch's January 2025 Series A funding round, which valued the company at $85 million.

This potential acquisition marks Palo Alto Networks' seventh deal of the year, underscoring a corporate strategy of acquiring rather than building internal solutions to address AI-driven cybersecurity threats. The company has been highly active in the M&A market, having recently acquired Console for $500 million, Embrace for $325 million, and Koi for $231 million. The broader cybersecurity sector is seeing intense consolidation in the AI-agent security space, evidenced by Cyera’s $1 billion acquisition of Oasis Security and Cisco’s $400 million purchase of Astrix.
takeaways: **Deal Valuation:** The proposed $500 million cash deal for Clutch Security represents a 50x multiple on the startup's $10 million ARR.
**Recent Funding:** Clutch Security was last valued at $85 million during a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire.
**Palo Alto M&A Velocity:** This potential transaction is the seventh acquisition by Palo Alto Networks in 2025, following previous purchases of Console, Embrace, Chronosphere, and Koi.

**Competitive Landscape:** The AI agent security market is consolidating rapidly, with comparable acquisitions including Cyera’s $1 billion purchase of Oasis Security and Cisco’s $400 million acquisition of Astrix.

title: Contextual Pictograms for Repairing Multilingual ASR Errors
author: Mariana Hernandez, Hector Luna, Carlos Bruno, Luis Ricardo Santos, Elena Simoes
contentSnippet:
Authors: Mariana Hernandez , Hector Luna , Carlos Bruno , Luis Ricardo Santos , Elena Simoes

Abstract: Speech transcription errors can be difficult to recognize when competing word hypotheses are unfamiliar or visually similar. We describe an interface that combines alternative transcripts, replay and contextually checked pictograms for selected uncertain concepts. The system will initially support French and Spanish functional utterances. A counterbalanced study will assess whether pictorial feedback helps listeners recover the speaker's intended action beyond text alternatives alone. We will also quantify semantic mismatch and additional interaction time, since an inappropriate image can reinforce the wrong interpretation rather than repair it.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Mariana Hernandez, Hector Luna, Carlos Bruno, Luis Ricardo Santos, and Elena Simoes have introduced a novel interface designed to mitigate multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) errors. The system functions by augmenting traditional text-based transcriptions with alternative word hypotheses, audio replay capabilities, and contextually verified pictograms for specific, high-uncertainty concepts. The initial implementation focuses on functional utterances within French and Spanish language models.

The research methodology centers on a counterbalanced study designed to evaluate whether visual pictorial feedback improves a listener's ability to recover a speaker's intended meaning compared to text-only alternatives. A critical component of the evaluation involves quantifying semantic mismatch and the impact of additional interaction time, specifically testing the hypothesis that an incorrect or poorly matched image could potentially reinforce transcription errors rather than facilitate their repair.
takeaways: **System Components:** The interface integrates three primary modalities: alternative text transcripts, audio replay, and contextually checked pictograms.
**Language Support:** The initial deployment and testing phase is restricted to French and Spanish functional utterances.
**Evaluation Metrics:** The study measures the efficacy of pictorial feedback against semantic mismatch rates and the overhead of additional user interaction time.
**Core Hypothesis:** The research aims to determine if visual cues provide superior error recovery for unfamiliar or visually similar word hypotheses compared to text-based correction alone.

title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
author: Christian Clason, Tapio Helin, Medet Nursultanov, Lauri Oksanen
contentSnippet:
Authors: Christian Clason , Tapio Helin , Medet Nursultanov , Lauri Oksanen

Abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Christian Clason, Tapio Helin, Medet Nursultanov, and Lauri Oksanen have introduced AutoIP, a Lean library designed to formalize classical linear regularization theory and its underlying functional analysis. By leveraging AI agents to autoformalize mathematical proofs, the project aims to reduce the labor-intensive nature of proof verification. The library is structured to shift the human burden from proof-reading to statement-validation, where reviewers only need to verify that the formal Lean statements accurately reflect their intended natural-language mathematical counterparts.

The authors argue that the primary risk in formalization lies in the accuracy of the statements themselves rather than the logic of the proofs. Through the use of AutoIP, the team identified flaws in established textbook theorems, specifically uncovering a case where a theorem's hypothesis was more restrictive than the final assertion. The project serves as an open invitation for the inverse problems community to contribute to the library, utilizing machine-checked proofs to ensure mathematical rigor while automating the generation of the proofs themselves.
takeaways: **Project Name:** AutoIP, a Lean library for formalizing linear regularization theory and functional analysis.
**Methodology:** AI agents are used to autoformalize proofs, while human reviewers focus exclusively on verifying the accuracy of formal statements.

**Key Finding:** The authors identified a textbook theorem where the hypothesis was more restrictive than the stated conclusion, demonstrating the utility of automated testing in formalizing existing literature.
**Core Philosophy:** Machine-checked proofs certify the formal statement, shifting the human task from proof verification to intent validation.

title: KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
author: Zi-Jian Cheng, Weiming Wu, Jie Meng, Zhen Peng, Shan Huang, Qun Li, Guobing Wu, Lan-Zhe Guo
contentSnippet:
Authors: Zi-Jian Cheng , Weiming Wu , Jie Meng , Zhen Peng , Shan Huang , Qun Li , Guobing Wu , Lan-Zhe Guo

Abstract: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Zi-Jian Cheng, Weiming Wu, Jie Meng, Zhen Peng, Shan Huang, Qun Li, Guobing Wu, and Lan-Zhe Guo have introduced KDASO (Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization), a framework designed to improve liability adjudication tasks such as legal charge determination and ride-hailing dispute resolution. The system addresses three primary failures in current LLM-based adjudication: the obsolescence of static skill libraries, the 'semantic execution gap' where models deviate from expert logic, and the context-window limitations that prevent the use of large, comprehensive skill sets.

KDASO functions through a three-pronged mechanism: neighborhood-conditioned induction, which updates the skill library using recent adjudication data; execution-aligned refinement, which uses LLM trajectory analysis to align model behavior with expert logic; and context-budgeted routing to manage skill selection within limited token constraints. In empirical testing across legal liability and logical reasoning benchmarks, KDASO outperformed both general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. The framework demonstrated an 8.96% performance improvement in zero-shot transfer scenarios involving concept-similar tasks, highlighting the stability and transferability of the generated skills during continuous optimization cycles.
takeaways: **Core Mechanism:** KDASO utilizes neighborhood-conditioned induction, execution-aligned refinement, and context-budgeted routing to manage dynamic skill libraries.
**Performance Metric:** The framework achieved an 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar adjudication scenarios.
**Problem Domain:** The research specifically targets liability adjudication, including ride-hailing dispute resolution and legal charge determination.
**Systemic Fixes:** The model addresses the semantic execution gap and context-budget constraints that typically cause LLMs to omit critical domain-specific skills.

title: BlockLock: Reproducible LLM Inference with Fixed Batch Geometry
author: Xiuyuan Qi, Pedro Reviriego, Javier Conde, Shanshan Liu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Xiuyuan Qi , Pedro Reviriego , Javier Conde , Shanshan Liu

Abstract: Reproducible LLM inference requires that a request produces the same output regardless of the other requests in the batch. Existing solutions pay for this in different ways: batch-invariant kernels constrain every operator, and isolating prefill with fixed-shape decode ({our CoRun-style baseline}) gives up shared prefill compute and pads decode. We present BlockLock, which keeps shared batched prefill and pins only the numerical path of the protected request: it fixes the geometry that the request sees, with {two modes: BlockLock-Rows uses fixed-width rows and retains batched decode of all requests; BlockLock-Pack uses terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment, then extracts the protected request's KV state for target-only decode. Under a stated per-deployment contract, both modes preserve the target's output bitwise when its companions change.} Across five {dense} models (Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT) and three single-GPU deployments (NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100), we evaluate our approach on both tinyBenchmarks and BFCL{; we also include initial tensor-parallel experiments on two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Both modes preserve target sequences and Top20-logit bits in the reported tests.} At equal delivered work, {BlockLock-Rows} reduces latency by 53.5--55.0\% and improves throughput by 115.2--122.2\% relative to vLLM Batch-Invariant; compared with batch-invariant kernels, it needs no custom kernel implementations and constrains only the protected requests.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Xiuyuan Qi, Pedro Reviriego, Javier Conde, and Shanshan Liu have introduced BlockLock, a method for achieving bitwise-reproducible LLM inference without the performance penalties associated with existing batch-invariant kernels or isolated prefill strategies. By pinning the numerical path of a protected request while maintaining shared batched prefill, BlockLock ensures output consistency even when companion requests in a batch change. The system operates via two primary modes: BlockLock-Rows, which utilizes fixed-width rows to retain batched decode, and BlockLock-Pack, which employs terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment to extract KV state for target-only decoding.

Evaluated across five dense models—Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT—on NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100 GPUs, BlockLock demonstrates significant performance gains over vLLM Batch-Invariant. Specifically, BlockLock-Rows achieves a 53.5% to 55.0% reduction in latency and a 115.2% to 122.2% improvement in throughput at equal delivered work. Unlike batch-invariant kernels, BlockLock requires no custom kernel implementations and limits constraints strictly to the protected requests, while maintaining bitwise output and Top20-logit consistency across both single-GPU and tensor-parallel (dual A6000) configurations.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** BlockLock-Rows improves throughput by 115.2%–122.2% and reduces latency by 53.5%–55.0% compared to vLLM Batch-Invariant.
**Operating Modes:** The system uses two modes: BlockLock-Rows (fixed-width rows with batched decode) and BlockLock-Pack (terminal-anchored packing with isolated dummy segments).
**Model Compatibility:** The method was validated on Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT.
**Hardware Support:** Testing was conducted on NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100 GPUs, including initial tensor-parallel experiments on dual A6000s.
**Key Advantage:** Unlike batch-invariant kernels, BlockLock avoids custom kernel implementations and only constrains the specific protected request.

title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement Learning Post-Training through Elastic Expert Parallelism
author: Jia Wei, Ziyi Qiu, Yi Xu, Xuehai Qian
contentSnippet:
Authors: Jia Wei , Ziyi Qiu , Yi Xu , Xuehai Qian

Abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses is a major computational bottleneck. In mixture-of-experts models, workers that finish their assigned responses may remain occupied because their experts are still needed by workers processing longer responses. Consequently, approximately one-third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after local response generation finishes. Here we present FlexFloor, a system that enables earlier resource release during synchronous response generation while preserving the expert computation required by ongoing responses. FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers. It uses historical response lengths and memory constraints to guide batching and prompt placement, then progressively releases workers while maintaining expert availability and correct communication. Compared with the verl baseline, FlexFloor generates approximately 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied computing time and increases response generation throughput by 52.74%, with little observed variation in rollout reward. By making reinforcement learning post-training more efficient, FlexFloor supports faster development and iterative improvement of large language models and AI agents.

Notes: 19 pages including references and appendices, 5 figures

summary.tldr:
FlexFloor, a system developed by Jia Wei, Ziyi Qiu, Yi Xu, and Xuehai Qian, addresses the computational inefficiencies inherent in reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for mixture-of-experts (MoE) large language models. The authors identify that in standard synchronous generation, workers remain occupied even after completing their specific response tasks because their assigned experts are still required by other workers processing longer sequences. This bottleneck results in approximately one-third of total worker time being wasted post-completion.

FlexFloor optimizes this process by enabling earlier resource release through a joint adaptation of response scheduling and active worker grouping. By leveraging historical response length data and memory constraints, the system dynamically manages batching and prompt placement. This allows the framework to progressively release workers while ensuring that necessary expert computations remain available for ongoing tasks. Benchmarks against the verl baseline demonstrate that FlexFloor achieves a 65.40% increase in response tokens generated per unit of occupied computing time and a 52.74% improvement in overall response generation throughput, all while maintaining consistent rollout reward performance.
takeaways: **Efficiency Gains:** FlexFloor improves response generation throughput by 52.74% compared to the verl baseline.
**Resource Utilization:** The system increases response tokens generated per unit of occupied computing time by 65.40%.
**Core Mechanism:** FlexFloor utilizes historical response length data and memory constraints to dynamically schedule prompts and release workers early.
**Performance Parity:** The implementation maintains rollout reward performance with little observed variation compared to standard methods.

title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
author: Vivek Acharya
contentSnippet:
Authors: Vivek Acharya

Abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. A simulation with known ground truth shows the spine sustaining cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero, the reconciliation residual recovering planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors, and mid-flight gating cutting p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate. We propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.

Notes: 16 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables. Code and synthetic data: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Vivek Acharya introduces the 'Two-Ledger Model,' a framework designed to bridge the gap between high-level settlement-grain billing data and granular, invocation-level AI usage in multi-agent systems. Current standards like the FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) aggregate costs by SKU and billing period, failing to map AI expenditures to specific business outcomes like individual orders or claims. The proposed model joins a FOCUS-conformant settlement ledger with an attribution ledger derived from OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry, utilizing a 'correlation spine'—comprising trace context, Model Context Protocol (MCP) metadata, and business-key matching—to assign costs to specific transactions.

The architecture employs a versioned rate card for near-real-time pricing and a reconciliation process that ties both ledgers to actual invoices, effectively isolating 'shadow AI' spend. Simulations demonstrate that the correlation spine maintains over 99% cost coverage even when trace propagation fails. Furthermore, the model enables mid-flight cost gating, which reduced p99 transaction costs by up to 61% in testing, albeit with a 2-4% false-pause rate. The author proposes that this attribution ledger be adopted as an invocation-grain profile within the FOCUS standard to standardize how enterprises track AI-driven business costs.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** The Two-Ledger Model joins settlement-grain FOCUS billing data with invocation-grain attribution records via a multi-layered correlation spine.

**Performance Metrics:** Simulations show the spine maintains >99% cost coverage even with zero trace propagation, while reconciliation residuals identified unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points.
**Operational Efficiency:** Mid-flight cost gating achieved a p99 transaction cost reduction of up to 61% with a 2-4% false-pause rate.
**Standardization Proposal:** The author advocates for the attribution ledger to be formalized as an invocation-grain profile within the existing FOCUS specification.

title: Autonomous AI Agents Systematically Diverge From Human Preferences in Proof Formalization
author: B\'alint Gyevn\'ar, Simon DeDeo
contentSnippet:
Authors: Bálint Gyevnár , Simon DeDeo

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have ushered in a new age of proof abundance, but helping humans understand these proofs requires new attention to the differences in how AI agents and humans pursue a proof-making task. We present "simulated collaboration", a methodology that allows us to examine two key questions: (1) the relative attention AI agents pay to surface syntax or, conversely, deeper underlying semantics, and (2) how and where AI agent preferences for what to do next diverge from human preferences. On a set of nine major human collaborations in Lean with 4.7M definitions across more than 6K commits, we find that, over the course of proof construction, AI agents (1) are far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps; (2) show a relative aversion to densely connected proof centers and to complex or surprising proof goals; and (3) are relatively attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to regularize toward baseline. Our results highlight important blind spots and potential interventions for future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Bálint Gyevnár and Simon DeDeo have introduced a 'simulated collaboration' methodology to analyze the divergence between AI agents and human mathematicians in the Lean proof assistant environment. By evaluating nine major human collaborations comprising 4.7 million definitions across over 6,000 commits, the study identifies fundamental differences in how AI agents prioritize proof construction compared to human experts.

The findings indicate that AI agents exhibit a strong bias toward explicitly marked gaps while demonstrating a distinct aversion to densely connected proof centers and complex, surprising proof goals. Conversely, the agents show an attraction to surprising proof bodies, which they systematically attempt to regularize toward baseline patterns. These results suggest that AI agents prioritize surface-level syntax and predictable structures over the deeper semantic strategies favored by human mathematicians, highlighting critical blind spots in current automated proof-making systems.
takeaways: **Dataset Scope:** The study analyzed 4.7 million definitions across more than 6,000 commits from nine major human collaborations in the Lean proof assistant.
**AI Bias:** AI agents show a significantly higher propensity than humans to focus on explicitly marked gaps during proof construction.
**Structural Aversion:** Agents demonstrate a relative aversion to complex proof goals and densely connected proof centers.
**Regularization Tendency:** AI agents are attracted to surprising proof bodies but tend to regularize them toward baseline, indicating a preference for predictable syntax over semantic complexity.

title: Trust Responsive Runtime Authorization for Agentic AI with Empirical Characterization of Policy Behavior and Parameter Sensitivity
author: Ahsan Habib Shihab, Imre Felde, Ramis Akhmedov, Stefan Gubo, Berik Sabdenaliyev, Madina Mansurova, Amir Mosavi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.06996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The policy that converts runtime estimates of an autonomous agent's condition into operational authority is rarely specified or measured. We empirically characterize the Trust Responsive Authorization Policy (TRAP), which maps an Authorization Readiness Score (ARS), a weighted combination of runtime trust, operational stability, and contextual risk, onto discrete authorization levels through an asymmetric rule: escalation requires consecutive observations above a band edge plus a margin, while a sharp drop in readiness restricts authority at once. On one matched set of 100 Monte Carlo traces, we compare TRAP with static, trust-only, risk-only, and symmetric policies. Under abrupt degradation, TRAP restricts at onset and re-escalates sooner after recovery than the symmetric policy, with the highest and, descriptively, least variable stability among the adaptive policies, although more of its post-recovery escalations occur below the selected trust threshold. Paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero for the remaining differences. In one-factor sweeps, recovery time rises with the escalation margin and run length, shifts with the score weights, and is unchanged by the restriction threshold. In an exploratory post-freeze experiment, when the same degradation is spread over 5-20 intervals, TRAP restricts only on the 4 traces that retain a single-interval drop above that threshold; averaged over all 100 traces, it holds authority above what readiness supports for 15.9-18.9 of the 20 degradation intervals, against 0.8 under abrupt degradation and about 10 for the symmetric policy. Its restriction advantage therefore depends on degradation being abrupt. All reported values are traceable to the publicly available, versioned research release.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced the Trust Responsive Authorization Policy (TRAP), a framework designed to manage operational authority for autonomous agents by mapping an Authorization Readiness Score (ARS) to discrete authorization levels. The ARS is calculated as a weighted combination of runtime trust, operational stability, and contextual risk. TRAP utilizes an asymmetric rule set: authority escalation requires consecutive observations exceeding a specific band edge plus a margin, whereas authority restriction occurs immediately upon a sharp drop in readiness. This mechanism aims to balance safety with performance by ensuring rapid restriction during failures while maintaining stability during recovery.

In a comparative study using 100 Monte Carlo traces, TRAP was evaluated against static, trust-only, risk-only, and symmetric policies. TRAP demonstrated superior stability and faster re-escalation post-recovery compared to symmetric policies. However, the study noted that TRAP's restriction advantage is highly sensitive to the nature of degradation; it is effective during abrupt failures but significantly less so during gradual degradation (spread over 5-20 intervals). In gradual scenarios, TRAP maintained authority levels above what the readiness score supported for 15.9-18.9 of 20 intervals, compared to only 0.8 intervals during abrupt degradation.
takeaways: **Policy Mechanism:** TRAP uses an asymmetric rule where escalation requires consecutive observations above a threshold plus a margin, while restriction is immediate upon a sharp readiness drop.
**Performance Metrics:** TRAP exhibited the highest and least variable stability among adaptive policies tested in 100 Monte Carlo simulations.

**Sensitivity Analysis:** One-factor sweeps revealed that recovery time increases with escalation margin and run length, shifts with score weights, but remains unaffected by the restriction threshold.
**Degradation Limitation:** TRAP's restriction advantage is contingent on abrupt degradation; during gradual degradation, it held authority above supported levels for up to 18.9 out of 20 intervals.

title: Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI
author: Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development. The central challenge is not simply to accelerate the evolution of intelligence, but to preserve humanity's ability to guide its direction, limit its speed, and intervene when necessary.

summary.tldr:
The paper 'Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI' (arXiv:2611.07048v1) introduces a theoretical framework to analyze how AI agents might direct their own evolutionary trajectories. The authors categorize evolutionary mechanisms into three distinct models: Darwinian (natural selection), Lamarckian (inherited learning), and agent-directed (self-generated behavioral variants). The study finds that as learning effectiveness increases, these mechanisms demonstrate progressively faster adaptation rates, with agent-directed evolution offering the highest potential for rapid improvement through self-evaluation and search optimization.

Technically, the framework posits that optimal search effort is a function of learning capability, problem complexity, and the cost of experimentation. While increased variant generation accelerates adaptation, the authors identify a critical failure mode: if an agent's evaluation target is misspecified, the system will rapidly converge toward incorrect behaviors despite showing improved performance metrics. In recursive self-improvement scenarios, these errors can propagate across generations, creating significant AI safety risks. The authors conclude that autonomous AI development requires independent oversight mechanisms that scale proportionally with the agent's ability to self-modify, ensuring that human objectives remain the primary constraint on evolutionary direction and speed.

**Performance Trade-off:** Increased search effort and variant generation accelerate adaptation but exacerbate the risk of converging on misspecified objectives.
**Safety Risk:** Recursive self-improvement can lock in evaluation errors across generations, making human intervention increasingly difficult as agents become more autonomous.
**Oversight Requirement:** The authors argue that independent evaluation must scale alongside autonomous development to maintain control over the speed and direction of AI evolution.

title: Closed-Loop Agent Evaluation: Layered Measurement and Self-Calibration
author: Ruifeng Ren, Gun Ahn
contentSnippet:
Authors: Ruifeng Ren , Gun Ahn

Abstract: Once an agent is live, teams want to know whether it is doing its job, not just whether it throws errors. Yet most evaluation is one-off: a benchmark run, a look at traces, a single score. Its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent. We propose closed-loop evaluation, an evaluation method for deployed agents. It models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and it requires every level's conclusion to trace back to atomic data and to be computed by versioned rules. The method covers four levels of analysis (span, trace, conversation and engagement), measures along a spine of Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, treats Conduct as a constraint throughout, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components to certify the evidence and the evaluators. Evaluator agents generated by an Agent Factory carry these components, each with a domain knowledge pack and an adapter harness. Two loops close the evaluation: an inner loop audits the evidence, rules and metrics themselves, and an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. We also give a pipeline that runs this process automatically. Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, we show how problems differ across levels and how evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring (ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81; kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63).

Notes: 7 pages

summary.tldr:
Researchers Ruifeng Ren and Gun Ahn have introduced 'Closed-Loop Agent Evaluation,' a framework designed to move beyond static, one-off benchmarking for deployed AI agents. The method treats evaluation as a performance estimation problem under conditions of biased raters and censored outcomes, requiring all conclusions to be traceable to atomic data via versioned rules. The system is structured across four analytical levels—span, trace, conversation, and engagement—and evaluates performance along four primary dimensions: Execution, Substance, Trajectory, and Results, with Conduct maintained as a constant constraint.

The architecture utilizes an 'Agent Factory' to generate evaluator agents equipped with domain-specific knowledge packs and adapter harnesses. These evaluators incorporate Provenance and Adjudication components to certify evidence. The framework operates through two feedback loops: an inner loop that audits the integrity of evidence, rules, and metrics, and an outer loop that employs per-component regression checks to facilitate iterative agent improvement. The authors validated the method using a business-analysis agent named SharpInsight and public conversation data, demonstrating that evidence-and-rule-based judgment significantly outperforms holistic scoring, achieving an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) of 0.86 compared to 0.81, and a kappa score of 0.81 versus 0.63.
takeaways: **Evaluation Dimensions:** The framework measures performance across four pillars: Execution, Substance, Trajectory, and Results, while treating Conduct as a mandatory constraint.
**Analytical Hierarchy:** Evaluation is conducted across four distinct levels of granularity: span, trace, conversation, and engagement.
**Performance Metrics:** The method demonstrated superior reliability over holistic scoring, achieving an ICC of 0.86 and a kappa of 0.81 in validation tests.
**System Architecture:** The pipeline utilizes an Agent Factory to deploy evaluator agents, which include specific components for Provenance and Adjudication to ensure evidence certification.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration
author: Sungil Son, Hoseong Jung, Dahyun Oh, H. Jin Kim
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.

title: When Verification Is Not Agreement: Cross-Agent LLM-to-Dafny Formalization
author: Priyanath Maji
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A verified Dafny postcondition certifies that a formula holds, but it does not guarantee that the result was reached through genuine independent reasoning. We introduce a cross-agent formalization protocol where a Specifier model translates clinical trial criteria into a Dafny predicate, and an Implementer model writes an operational method checked against it. A same-model control establishes that even with no capability gap, independent re-extraction from identical text agrees only 59.3% of the time. Evaluating four model configurations on 96 clinical trial documents, we find that agreement is highly sensitive to how model capability is allocated across the two roles: the GPT-4.1-nano/GPT-4.1-mini configuration achieves 53.0% agreement when the stronger model is the Implementer, but only 14.3% when the roles are reversed. The strongest tested configuration, GPT-5.6-luna/GPT-5.4-mini, improves agreement to 34.4% but remains below the same-model baseline and is dominated by direct contradiction (42.7%). We also detect a critical verification artifact in which a weaker Implementer satisfies the postcondition by invoking the Specifier's predicate directly; after structural auditing, corrected agreement falls from 14.3% to 13.2%. Our results show that verification success alone is insufficient evidence of independent cross-agent agreement, and that model capability does not guarantee agreement when formalizing the same source independently.

title: Synthesizing symbolic models of human and machine reasoning at scale
author: Solim LeGris, Philipp Mondorf, Jinran Jin, Akshay K. Jagadish, Brenden M. Lake, Todd M. Gureckis
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symbolic models offer a powerful account of cognition, but their scope has historically been limited by the need for hand-engineering and computational tractability. We show how advances in artificial intelligence (AI) can scale symbolic modeling and help overcome these engineering limitations. We introduce Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS)---an approach for automated search of interpretable, deterministic symbolic programs that verifiably reproduce behavior---and apply it to model both human and machine behavior across hundreds of challenging reasoning problems. Analyzing these programs reveals that both people and machines tend to oversimplify, adopt rules that are partial explanations for their observations, and misinfer dependencies between problem features. These shared signatures are modulated by available resources, with reasoning effort predicting the extent to which machines simplify and explain their observations. Together, these results point to underlying mechanisms reminiscent of satisficing in both people and machines, and illustrate how BCSS offers a general approach for interpreting and comparing rule-based reasoning of humans and black-box AI systems.

title: PromptOps: Iterative Prompt Optimization for LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
author: Sven Kleinkop, Tam\'as Janusko, Ricardo Bochnia, Gunnar Hempel, Steffen Tomschke, J\"urgen Anke, Maik Thiele
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for evaluating the behavior of chatbots and other AI systems. In deployment, however, their agreement with the intended human evaluation policy may degrade as user interactions and score distributions change. Existing automatic prompt optimization methods are primarily studied as one-shot procedures on static development sets and therefore provide limited guidance for maintaining LLM judges over time. We frame this problem as judge drift and introduce PromptOps, a closedloop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaaJ) systems. PromptOps separates four operational decisions: when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt. We instantiate the framework with five prompt optimization methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that iterative prompt optimization can recalibrate LLM judges and recover performance after controlled shifts in the referencescore distribution. However, effective maintenance is inherently contextdependent: neither optimization algorithm choice nor update timing generalizes universally across settings. These findings establish prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an inherently iterative maintenance problem and demonstrate that PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing this process.

title: Goal Revelation as a Bridge Between Information-Theoretic Empowerment and Capability-Based Human Power
author: Jaime Ruiz-Serra, Tom\'a\v{s} Gaven\v{c}iak, Jobst Heitzig
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power matters for AI safety. Optimal agents tend to acquire power across a wide range of objectives (instrumental convergence). As we embed AI agents into socio-technical systems, humans risk gradual disempowerment. Both concerns call for a formal, quantitative measure of power. Two such measures in the context of Markov games are information-theoretic empowerment, the capacity of the channel from an agent's actions to future states, and capability-based individual power, a measure of goal attainment built from the probabilities that a human would attain each goal in a family of candidates were they pursuing it. We show where the two meet. From individual power, Fano's inequality yields a floor $B(s)$. This floor is a lower bound on what we term goal revelation, the mutual information $\mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s)$ between the human's latent goal and the realised trajectory. Empowerment caps revelation from above, so that $B(s) \le \mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s) \le \mathbb{I}(\mathbf{A}_h \to \xi \mid s) \le \mathfrak{E}_h(s)$. Each quantity can be large while the one below it stays at zero, highlighting the following failure modes. An assistant maximising empowerment can prefer an interface offering broad influence over goal-irrelevant degrees of freedom to one that lets the human attain every goal they might hold. An assistant maximising revelation cannot tell a working interface from one rewired so that every goal yields the wrong outcome, since relabelling goals leaves mutual information unchanged while zeroing every attainment probability. Positive guarantees therefore come only from the attainment end of the chain. A satisfaction floor, computable from two statistics of interaction logs, offers a way to monitor the power users retain in a deployed system, and simulations in random environments show the three quantities are correlated but far from interchangeable.

title: Robust Ranking of Port Impacts from Impending Tropical Cyclones: A Two-Stage Recommendation System
author: Chenchen Kuai, Shixuan Tang, Chaolun Ma, Xiaoqiang Kong, Xiubin Bruce Wang, Yunlong Zhang, Zihao Li
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a tropical cyclone (TC) threatens several ports, preparedness planning depends on anticipating which ports are likely to be affected and where disruptions may last longest. Limited historical observations at individual ports and uncertainty in landfall location make these relative impacts difficult to estimate. We use a two-stage recommendation framework that first selects candidate ports based on their proximity to the expected landfall location and then ranks them by their estimated number of impact days. Using AIS-derived impact days for 37 ports and 31 TCs in the Gulf of Mexico study region, we compare three ways of representing port--cyclone interactions: pairwise feature interactions, tree-based feature combinations, and explicit feature crosses combined with learned embeddings. In tests on Hurricanes Nicole and Ian, the retrieval stage consistently identifies all observed affected ports under landfall uncertainty. Among the ranking models, Wide & Deep Learning achieves the closest agreement with the observed port rankings. Its mean ranking agreement exceeds that of the distance-based baseline by 85.5% for Nicole and 55.5% for Ian and is less sensitive to uncertainty in the landfall location. These rankings could help port authorities prioritize post-cyclone inspections and allocate recovery resources across ports threatened by the same event.

title: EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments
author: Mingxuan Li, Huanzhi Mao, Qiuyang Mang, Hanchen Li, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Alex Dimakis
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An LLM agent's cost and success depend on its model, its harness, and its environment. In addition to the widely studied directions of parameter tuning and harness optimization, we propose the third direction: optimization over stationary environments. Agents are often deployed in rich environments shared by many tasks, such as a company's Slack workspace or a complex collection of data sources, documents or tickets. We call these environments stationary environments. We introduce EnvOpt, a method for automated end-to-end optimization of stationary environments for any given model and harness, using real or synthetic tasks without needing any graders or reference answers. On AutomationBench, EnvOpt reduces the cost of Claude Haiku 4.5 by 72.7% and raises its pass rate by 14.34%. The same environment transfers to Opus 5, cutting its cost by 68.1% with a 1.34% gain. Added on top of Meta-Harness's optimized harness for Haiku 4.5, it lowers cost by a further 83.4% and adds 11.17% accuracy over Meta-Harness alone. Across 5 benchmarks, EnvOpt significantly reduces the cost of agents while improving or maintaining pass rate, and is transferable to different models and different harnesses. We also discuss common successful and rejected environment optimization strategies during automated optimization. More broadly, our results show that how information is represented to an agent shapes both its cost and its success, making the environment worth optimizing in addition to the parameters and the harness.

title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance
author: Yupeng Cao, Xueqing Peng, Lingfei Qian, Haohang Li, Yangyang Yu, Anke Xu, Wenbo Cao, Yan Wang, Yuechen Jiang, Yuyan Wang, Zhuohan Xie, Yankai Chen, Zehan Li, Jimin Huang, Xue Liu, Jian-Yun Nie, Sophia Ananiadou
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.

title: SAVeR$^2$: Reasoning-based Safety Alignment for Large Reasoning Models via Verifiable Rewards
author: Yichen Sun, Qirui Liu, Yan Wang, Jianan Lin, Linbo Jiang, Shiyu Wang, Zhibo Wang, Zhixuan Chu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.

title: DelegateEval: Evaluating Platforms for Personal External Service Agents
author: Jichao Li, Jinrong Lu, Manjiang Yu, Zhixuan Liu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents that work for an individual over time may also help that individual serve external clients. We define a personal external service agent as an agent authorized and continuously managed by a specific individual to accept client requests, deliver work, and provide ongoing support using that person's knowledge, experience, professional methods, and service boundaries. Such agents could allow individuals to serve more clients with less direct involvement and generate economic value at scale. These dimensions assess whether a platform enables people with different backgrounds to turn their expertise into ongoing services that deliver verifiable work, develop capabilities through experience, and remain economically feasible. We present the framework and an experimental design. Complete datasets, executable environments, a unified scoring protocol, and cross-model results remain to be developed and empirically validated.

title: Graph learning-assisted logic-based Benders decomposition for distributionally robust in-station train rescheduling under disruptions
author: Xiaobin Li, Yanbin Gao, Jianing Long, Wuming Lei
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncertainty in resource reopening times complicates train holding and rerouting decisions when resource closures coincide with arrival delays and processing-time extensions. We develop a rolling-horizon distributionally robust model that updates predictions of the remaining closure duration as observations of disruption resolution become available. The model jointly optimizes train routes, sequences, and timings. It minimizes the worst-case expected total completion delay over an ambiguity set of scenario probabilities. The solution algorithm, GNN-LBBD, uses logic-based Benders decomposition to coordinate routing and resource scheduling. Conditional cuts are constructed from resource-use patterns, and a graph neural network guides the order in which resource relaxation subproblems are solved. Across 28 test instances for a five-track station, GNN-LBBD achieved a mean total completion delay of 61.13 train-min. This was 16.63\% lower than tabu search and 20.06\% lower than variable neighborhood search, with a mean total computation time close to that of tabu search. Information comparisons on six representative instances showed that using observations of disruption resolution reduced mean total completion delay by approximately 21.7\%. Scenario-based and conditional-mean predictions produced similar overall results under the same information conditions. The benefits of information were more pronounced in some instances with alternative routes. This suggests a relationship between the use of observations, the station resource structure, and the scope for schedule adjustments.

title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
author: Aleksandr Volkov, Roman Sultimov, Mikhail Kuzin, Yury Maximov
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.06953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources. The effect of physics-derived features depended on the evaluation. They increased gradient-boosting $R^2$ by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis and decreased it by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis. We report group-level errors and a synthetic regression experiment illustrating how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. These results motivate reporting the evaluation population alongside a property estimate or compliance score.

title: Octopus: One Brain, Many Branches for Latent-KV Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
author: Tianming Sha
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.06956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems explore in parallel by spawning sub-agents with isolated context windows, whereas single-agent systems append every search and verification step into one growing trajectory. However, existing multi-agent frameworks duplicate prefix KV caches across branches, exchange findings by re-prefilling text summaries, and flatten or drop cross-branch dependencies during reinforcement learning (RL). We introduce Octopus, a single-model multi-agent RL framework in which all threads share one backbone and coordinate over a GPU-resident directed acyclic graph (DAG) of KV states through five primitives (fork, read_thread, wait_threads, rewind, commit). Octopus combines three co-designed mechanisms: (1) Zero-Copy Radix Forking, which spawns branches as $\mathcal{O}(1)$ cursor views over shared physical KV pages; (2) Attention-Only KV Mounting, which mounts a sibling thread's terminal KV blocks directly into full-attention layers while bypassing linear-recurrent states (Gated DeltaNet / Mamba-2), cutting off-task hijacking by $21\times$ ($57.9\% \to 2.7\%$) while retaining $92.2\%$ of full-text mutual information at zero extra KV allocation; and (3) a Packed DAG-GRPO Trainer, which packs all episode branches into one block-sparse attention pass and assigns counterfactual branch credit via leave-one-branch-out marginal rewards. Trained end-to-end with GRPO on Qwen3.5-4B over a sparse BM25 corpus, Octopus reaches $49.6\%$ accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus ($+17.5$ points over single-agent GRPO at 143K context and $+12.5$ points over text-summary multi-agent RL) and $51.2\%$ on OpenResearcher, outperforming dense-retrieval agents up to $250\times$ larger while increasing training throughput $3.3\times$ and cutting peak KV memory $2.8\times$.

title: Uncertainty calibration in Bayesian M/EEG source imaging
author: Ismail Huseynov, Mohammad Orabe, Srikantan Nagarajan, Stefan Haufe
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.06979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: M/EEG source imaging requires accurate localization and reliable uncertainty estimates, yet posterior credible regions are rarely assessed for empirical calibration. We present a simulation-based framework for uncertainty quantification and calibration of empirical Bayesian inverse methods with closed-form conditional Gaussian posterior summaries. We compare Bayesian minimum norm (BMN) with sLORETA depth weighting and sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) with sparse basis field expansions (S-FLEX). S-FLEX allows retained coefficients to contribute nonzero marginal posterior variance at locations where voxel-wise SBL yields degenerate variances. For BMN, we derive joint source- and noise-variance updates through evidence maximization. We test whether adaptive noise learning yields near-calibrated uncertainties. Both methods retain residual miscalibration, motivating post-hoc isotonic recalibration of credible-region levels using empirical coverage. Simulations assess fixed- and free-orientation models across signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), source sparsity levels, and subject-specific head models, using oracle, baseline-estimated, and adaptively learned noise. Before recalibration, SBL+S-FLEX yields lower Wasserstein localization error, smaller posterior uncertainty, and coverage closer to nominal credibility than BMN+sLORETA. Isotonic recalibration improves both methods, with larger gains for conservative BMN+sLORETA posteriors; transfer across mismatched SNR, sparsity, and head models remains condition dependent. Noise specifications yield broadly consistent reconstruction and uncertainty trends within each estimator. In real auditory MEG data, SBL+S-FLEX provides more focal localization and tighter uncertainties than BMN+sLORETA, suggesting greater statistical power for identifying bilateral auditory sources.

title: Big Models, Small Gains: Frozen Forecasters as Classifiers on MONSTER
author: Rishit Jain, Rishit Kar, Chetashri Bhadane, Nilesh Patil
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.06988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forecasting foundation models are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for time series classification, but it remains unclear whether their pretrained representations offer an advantage over strong classifiers that do not require pretraining. This raises an important question: do these representations provide useful information beyond what the model architecture alone can capture, particularly when labelled data are scarce? We present a controlled benchmarking of two forecasting models, Reverso and Chronos-Bolt, on six large datasets from the MONSTER benchmark, using 1%, 10%, and 100% of the available training labels. We compare their frozen representations against four established time series classification methods and random-weight versions of the same forecasting models. Our results show that pretraining improves classification accuracy over random-weight counterparts on five of the six datasets, with gains of up to 23 percentage points. However, the frozen representations do not reliably outperform the strongest non-pretrained baseline in any setting: they perform worse in 15 of 17 settings and tie in the remaining two. Further experiments show that restoring amplitude information recovers part of the performance gap, while fine-tuning and forecast-error features do not close it. These findings highlight the importance of strong task specific baselines and random weight controls when evaluating forecasting foundation models for classification. Our code is available at https://github.com/Rachet2006/frozen-forecasters-monster.

title: Robust Stream Classification using Time Neutralising Decision Trees
author: Brandon Gower-Winter, Georg Krempl
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.06991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data Streams are characterised as a potentially infinite source of data subject to non-stationarity. This non-stationarity, also called Concept Drift, often results in deployed predictive models having to be perpetually retrained as the underlying data generating process of the stream changes over time. Drift Detectors are a class of methods used to identify these changes, triggering these retraining procedures. Historically, Stream Learning has operated under the assumption that instances are only seen once, and cannot be stored for later use. Contemporary work relaxes this assumption, yet drift detection and simple resetting procedures are still ubiquitous. Building on related work which has shown that traditional Batch Learning algorithms often outperform Stream Learning algorithms when instances can be stored, we introduce Time Neutralising Trees (TNT), a Decision Tree architecture that enables robust stream classification in settings with Concept Drift. During training, TNT will filter out ("neutralise") old training samples that are no longer relevant given the current context of the stream. If those instances become relevant again, TNT will then re-include them. We evaluate TNT, and related algorithms on 24 real and semi-real classification data streams from the USP DS repository. Results show strong evidence that TNT achieves best-in-class performance on a wide-range of data streams with varying concept drift types.

title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time
author: Teresa Delgado, Hugo Hazard, Martin Benfeghoul, Jun Wang, Zafeirios Fountas
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.

title: Stochastic Dynamics of Generative AI: From Autoregressive Models to Interacting LLM Networks and Neural SDEs
author: Vikram Krishnamurthy, Yiming Zhang, Luke Snow
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a stochastic dynamical-systems perspective on three classes of generative AI models. First, we formulate large language models (LLMs) as high-dimensional nonlinear autoregressive models with attention-based dependencies. This formulation connects pretraining by conditional maximum likelihood to sequential token generation and provides a probabilistic interpretation of LLM operation. Second, we consider networks of interacting LLMs and characterize their collective behavior through mean-field ordinary differential equations. These dynamics provide a framework for understanding emergent preferential attachment and persistent structural biases, including type-dependent glass-ceiling effects. Third, we consider neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs) as continuous-time generative models for stochastic trajectories, including those observed at irregular time intervals. We discuss their training with particular emphasis on Wiener-space cubature methods based on rough-path analysis as an efficient alternative to Monte Carlo estimation. Together, the three settings address probabilistic prediction, information exchange and emergent behavior in interacting networks, and path-space generative modeling.

title: Finite-Time Convergence and Regret Guarantees for Neural Reinforcement Learning in POMDPs
author: Jingjuan Huang, Zhiyao Zhang, Alvaro Velasquez, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Jia Liu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) is computationally challenging due to the curse of long-range dependence on history. Fortunately, recent studies have shown that a range of POMDPs that satisfy the filter stability assumption can be well approximated by a superstate Markov Decision Process (MDP) based on a truncated history in a finite-memory window, with a value gap that decays with the window length. However, existing finite-time convergence analyses on such superstate MDP surrogates are either limited to over-simplified linear function approximation or rely on an i.i.d. sampling oracle that is violated by POMDP trajectories, both of which severely limit the applicability of these theoretical results in practice. This motivates us to bridge the gap by investigating RL in POMDPs with nonlinear neural value function approximation. Our main contributions are threefold: i) We first establish a new finite-state MDP point-wise approximation error bound, which lays the foundation for our RL algorithm design and analysis in POMDPs; ii) By applying Temporal-Difference (TD) learning to POMDP-generated superstate transitions and targeting the Bellman fixed point of the superstate MDP, we prove a finite-time critic error bound with nonlinear neural value function approximation; and iii) By combining the neural critic function approximation error bound with the policy mirror descent framework, we obtain a finite-time sublinear regret against the optimal POMDP value. To the best of our knowledge, such a finite-time sublinear regret based on neural function approximation is the first in the literature for finite-memory POMDPs. Our numerical experiments also verify our theoretical results.

title: Shaping & Monitoring Models through their Internal Representations
author: Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal, Matt Feiszli, Satchel Grant, Andrew Lee, Chris Earls, Fatih Dinc, Vasudev Shyam, Usha Bhalla, Leon Bergen, Siddharth Boppana, Ching Fang, Michael Byun, Tristan Gallent, Nicholas Wang, Tal Haklay, Dron Hazra, Neehar Kondapaneni, Connor Watts, Ryan Panwar, Thomas Dooms, Jack Merullo, Atticus Geiger, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Thomas McGrath, Owen Lewis
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose Mechanistic Shaping, a unified framework for shaping models through their internal representations. Mechanistic Shaping is applied during training so that models follow specifications (rules) about which concepts they express, measured via their outputs or internal representations (e.g., no harmful content), and also which concepts they rely on, i.e., what they use to make their decisions (e.g., not a candidate's gender when screening a r\'esum\'e). Across multiple domains (vision, medical imaging, language), scales (up to 32B parameters), and training paradigms (classification, SFT, DPO, GRPO), we find that Mechanistic Shaping substantially reduces targeted behaviors while preserving task performance. Since training against a representation can also modify it, we ask whether shaped concepts remain monitorable, a question that depends on the class of monitors considered. We therefore introduce a hierarchy of such classes, which separates a concept that escapes one probe from a concept that is truly gone. We characterize three geometric mechanisms of circumvention: the concept can drift away from the monitor, be erased from the layer, or persist in higher-order statistics as a nonlinear encoding, which we explain through a product-code construction. Although other mechanisms may arise in different settings or at larger scales, these three account for all of our observations, and each can be detected by a matching monitor. In practice, we find that shaped concepts largely remain monitorable: refitted linear probes recover the concept in most settings, and the original probe remains reliable whenever gradients do not flow through it. Taken together, these results point to the potential of using interpretability as a tool for training, and call for a correspondingly rigorous science of interpretability-based training.

title: Optimistic Hedge in General-Sum Games: Fundamental Limits and Regret Bounds via Temporal Approximation
author: Yuval Dagan, Nadav Eisen, Liad Erez, Tomer Koren
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimistic Hedge, a multiplicative weight update with one step of extrapolation, is one of the most natural regret-minimizing dynamics for games, and characterizing its regret has been a longstanding open question. Daskalakis, Fishelson and Golowich proved that if all $m$ players in a finite general-sum game follow Optimistic Hedge with a fixed learning rate, each player's regret is polylogarithmic in the horizon $T$. Subsequently, Ha showed that an appropriate choice of learning rate makes each player's regret bounded independently of $T$. This bound, however, is non-constructive and its dependence on the number of actions $n$ is not explicit, leaving open whether Optimistic Hedge can achieve a constant regret bound which is polynomial in the size of the game. We show that the answer hinges on the number of players. In two-player games, there is a learning rate for which Optimistic Hedge guarantees $O(n\log n)$ regret independent of the horizon. In three-player games, however, no such bound is possible: for any learning rate up to an absolute constant and for sufficiently large horizon $T$, there is a game with $n$ actions per player in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(n)}$, and more generally, for every $m\ge3$ we construct $m$-player games in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(mn)}$; for learning rates above $2^{-\Omega(mn)}$, that player's regret even grows linearly in $T$. Our upper bound is based on a temporal approximation framework for the analysis of Optimistic Hedge. Starting from the variance-based RVU bound of Daskalakis et al., we approximate the losses over time-localized windows by well-behaved functions, whose total variation is a small fraction of their cumulative variance. In $m$-player games, the same framework gives a significantly simplified proof of the recent $O(\sqrt{m}\log n\log T)$ regret bound due to Ha.

title: Server-Side Sparse Assignment for Federated Mixture-of-Experts
author: Xue Zheng, Aylin Yener
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly recognized for their remarkable capabilities; federated learning (FL) offers a promising framework for collaboratively fine-tuning LLMs on edge devices while achieving data privacy. However, edge devices are inherently heterogeneous: clients may exhibit diverse data distributions and resource constraints, including limited memory and computation budgets. Recent federated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address these challenges by using sparse expert activation or partial expert loading. However, existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-specific relevant experts from partial observations. We propose $S^3$-MoE, a server-side sparse expert assignment framework that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit--explore mechanism. We also establish relevance-estimation error and exact Top-$K$ recovery guarantees. Experiments using a CNN-based MoE on CIFAR-100 show that $S^3$-MoE recovers task-dependent client--expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection across clients. Compared with Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client access to all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, $S^3$-MoE achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy while loading only $5$ experts per client.

title: A Night at the LLM Zoo: Data Conditioned Flow Matching for Generating Pretrained LLM Weights
author: Scott Biggs, Bedionita Soro, Saumya Gupta, Bruno Andreis, Sung Ju Hwang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.07103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A challenge to Weight Space Learning as it expands from task specific and vision models to Large Language Models (LLMs) is the absence of a well curated and analyzed LLM population. To address this, we train such a model zoo for application to Weight Space Generation by systematically varying the data mixture composition between web text, books, mathematics, coding, and French across populations of 51M, 124M, and 355M parameter GPT-2 Models, each tier with count N = 100. We analyze these populations by cosine similarity, functional diversity, Leave-One-Mixture-Out modeling, and variance decomposition. We show that the zoo contains diverse models whose variation is structured by training mixture composition. We embed the training mixture composition to condition a Flow Matching model of complete pretrained LLM weights in Gram-PCA compressed weight space. By demonstrating zero-shot generalization to held out mixtures, measuring Continuous Ranked Probability Score skill, as well as finding minimal changes in downstream test-set perplexity and general capability benchmark scores, we show that our generator generalizes on the simplex of data mixtures to produce models that perform similarly to those in the zoo ex nihilo. Finally, we produce all source code and artifacts to support the continued expansion of Weight Space Learning and Generation into the LLM domain.
