**Financial Performance:** Reported an annualized revenue run rate of over $800 million as of earlier this year.
**Operational Scale:** Employs 185 people and serves entertainment studios, advertising agencies, and game developers through a single API.
**Strategic Backing:** Nvidia participated in the round as a strategic investor; Bessemer Venture Partners led the round.
**Market Comparison:** Valuation is slightly lower than rival inference provider Fireworks AI, which is valued at $17.5 billion.

title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows
author: Aditya Mehta
contentSnippet:
Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday.

The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout.

For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said.

Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years , according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week .

In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s.

Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets.

In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April.

In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines.

Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity.

Converted jet en

summary.tldr:
AI data center operators are increasingly deploying converted jet engines to bypass multi-year grid connection delays, according to reports from the New York Times. By utilizing turbines salvaged from retired aircraft and retrofitted to burn natural gas, companies can achieve operational status in approximately 24 months. This timeline contrasts sharply with traditional grid infrastructure, which the International Energy Agency notes can take up to seven years to deliver 100 megawatts of power in regions like Northern Virginia.

Major industry players are actively adopting this stopgap measure. Elon Musk’s xAI has installed eight ProEnergy-rebuilt GE jet turbines at its Colossus 2 facility in Memphis, Mississippi. Similarly, OpenAI is utilizing gas turbines at its Stargate site in Abilene, Texas, a project managed by Denver-based startup Crusoe. While Crusoe previously considered a $1.25 billion deal for 29 turbines from Boom Supersonic, it ultimately pivoted to an order for 13 ProEnergy units in April 2025. These deployments are being encouraged by the current U.S. administration as a means to circumvent infrastructure bottlenecks.

Despite the speed of deployment, these converted engines present significant trade-offs. They are less fuel-efficient and generate higher emissions than purpose-built power plant turbines. Industry experts suggest that as environmental regulations and efficiency standards tighten, these jet-engine-based power solutions may prove to be a short-term strategy rather than a permanent infrastructure fix.
takeaways: **Deployment Speed:** Converted jet engines allow data centers to become operational in 24 months, compared to the seven-year wait times for standard grid connections.
**xAI Implementation:** xAI has deployed eight ProEnergy-rebuilt GE jet turbines to support the Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, Mississippi.
**OpenAI/Crusoe Project:** OpenAI’s Stargate site in Abilene, Texas, utilizes gas turbines, with Crusoe ordering 13 ProEnergy units for the campus in April 2025.
**Failed Deal:** Crusoe canceled a $1.25 billion agreement to purchase 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic in September.
**Operational Risks:** Converted jet engines are less efficient and more polluting than conventional power plant turbines, potentially limiting their long-term viability.

title: Anthropic Releases FlashProve: Cryptographic Proofs That a Reply Came From Committed Weights
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team has released FlashProve , an open-source research prototype for provable inference . FlashProve is a zkSNARK system from Anthropic that proves a reply came from a committed model. The proof reveals nothing about the model weights. On Llama 4 Maverick , a 400B mixture-of-experts model, it proves about 110 tokens/second on 1 H100. For developers, this targets a real gap: today you cannot check which model actually answered your API call. TL;DR Size: Proves a 400B MoE model (~17B active per token); context capped at 1,024 tokens per request. Runs on: Prover needs 1 H100 80 GB, 24 CPU cores and ~290 GB host RAM. Verifier runs on a CPU, no GPU. Performance: Orders of magnitude faster than prior open-source zkML systems on the same 400B model. Best: 110 tokens/second proving on 1 H100, with 18.78 MB proofs checked in 17 seconds. Worst: Proving costs ~70 to 95x the GPU time of plain vLLM inference. What problem does provable inference solve? A user querying a model cannot verify which model produced the response. A routing service could swap in a cheaper model . An attacker could tamper with the token stream. Judging from output quality alone is unreliable. Anthropic lists 4 use cases: Regulators could confirm hardware serves inference, supporting AI pacing rules. Labs could detect tampered inference servers. Users could verify text provenance. Regulators could enforce serving of approved models only. How does FlashProve work? FlashProve has a prover (the model provider) and a verifier (the user). It runs in 2 phases: Offline: The provider publishes a commitment, a short fingerprint binding one exact set of weights. This takes about 39 minutes and covers about 16 million requests. Online: For each request, the GPU produces a proof that the committed model produced those tokens. The proof system compiles an interactive oracle proof into a cryptographic proof using hash functions. Anthropic says this offers post-quantum security. It is the same family used by validity-proof L2 networks such as Starknet. Three engineering choices drive the speed. Prover work scales with the ~17B active parameters, not all 400B. Requests are proved in batches after the fact, like prefill. Weights stream from host memory, so a single 80 GB GPU suffices. How fast is it? Benchmarks Anthropic measured the public 4-bit Maverick weights on 1 H100 with 24 CPU cor

summary.tldr:
Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team has introduced FlashProve, an open-source zkSNARK-based research prototype designed to provide cryptographic verification that a specific model generated a given response. By utilizing a commitment scheme, the system allows providers to prove that a reply originated from a specific set of model weights without revealing the weights themselves. This addresses a critical transparency gap in the AI supply chain, where users currently lack the ability to verify if an API provider has swapped a high-performance model for a cheaper, lower-quality alternative or if the token stream has been tampered with.

Technically, FlashProve is optimized for large-scale models, specifically demonstrating performance on the 400B parameter Llama 4 Maverick mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, which utilizes approximately 17B active parameters per token. The system achieves a proving throughput of 110 tokens per second on a single H100 80GB GPU, with proofs sized at 18.78 MB that can be verified on a standard CPU in 17 seconds. While the proving process incurs a 70x to 95x GPU time overhead compared to standard vLLM inference, it utilizes post-quantum secure hash functions similar to those found in Starknet. The architecture relies on an offline phase—taking roughly 39 minutes to commit to 16 million requests—and an online phase where proofs are generated in batches.

FlashProve is positioned for use cases involving regulatory compliance, such as verifying that hardware is serving approved models, as well as enabling users to confirm text provenance and labs to detect tampered inference servers. The system requires significant host resources, including 24 CPU cores and 290 GB of host RAM, to manage the streaming of weights from host memory to the GPU, allowing the entire process to run on a single H100 node.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** Achieves 110 tokens/second proving speed on a 400B MoE model using a single H100 80GB GPU.
**Resource Requirements:** Prover node requires 1 H100 GPU, 24 CPU cores, and approximately 290 GB of host RAM.
**Verification Efficiency:** Generates 18.78 MB proofs that are verifiable on a standard CPU in 17 seconds.
**Operational Overhead:** Proving costs are 70 to 95 times higher in GPU time compared to standard vLLM inference.
**Security Foundation:** Utilizes post-quantum secure cryptographic proofs based on interactive oracle proofs, similar to L2 validity-proof networks.

title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers
author: Dar-Yen Chen, Yi-Zhe Song
contentSnippet: Adversarial diffusion distillation has conventionally relied on image features for discrimination. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs), whose text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention. We introduce Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which exploits intermediate text-token states as a new adversarial representation. Because the text stream has already read the image while remaining tied to the text condition, changing that condition changes what information it extracts from the image. Building on this property, we introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD), which conditions the discriminator on different aspects of the sample, such as typography, objects, or style, to steer which properties are emphasized during adversarial training. Building on the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion, we integrate TSAD and ACD in NitroFusion2. NitroFusion2 brings few-step distillation from the conventional 4-8-step regime down to just 1-2 steps at comparable quality. At one step, it produces sharp rendered text and rich fine-grained details, making one-step generation practical rather than merely a stress test for distillation. At two steps, it remains competitive across the evaluated benchmarks. These results establish the MMDiT text stream as a powerful and steerable representation for adversarial diffusion distillation.

title: NVIDIA Shows 3 Ways to Speed Up MoE Inference on DGX Spark, Lifting Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5%
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA’s latest technical blog shows how to speed up mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on one DGX Spark . The test model is Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling-3.0-flash , a 124B-parameter MoE with 5.1B active parameters. NVIDIA stacked three optimizations: a new MoE kernel backend, an FP8 output layer and built-in speculative decoding. On all 1,319 GSM8K questions, decode throughput rose 42.5% with no statistically detectable accuracy change. So why is it relevant for Devs? DGX Spark is a desktop system, not a data center node. NVIDIA’s results show a 124B MoE serving single-user requests faster on that desk-side box. The technical post also shows where MoE decode time goes, and how to cut it. TL;DR Size: Ling-3.0-flash-fp4: 124B total, 5.1B active per token; 256K native context. Runs on: One NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified memory, 273 GB/s), batch size one. Performance: Three stacked optimizations lift GSM8K decode throughput from 37.81 to 53.89 tokens/s. Best: +42.5% throughput and -24.5% mean latency, with accuracy flat (96.89% vs 96.82%). Lagging: Synthetic gains (+185.1%) shrink on GSM8K as MTP acceptance drops from 3.90 to 2.68. Why is MoE decoding on DGX Spark memory-bound? DGX Spark is NVIDIA’s desktop system built on the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip. It offers 128 GB of unified memory and 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth. Peak compute is up to 1 petaFLOP of sparse FP4. Decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out, the MoE computation and the LM head that scores the vocabulary. That points to two levers: move fewer bytes per decode step, and generate more tokens per verification round. The baseline followed the official W4A8 recipe. It used FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM and an FP32 LM-head path. On a synthetic 32K-input, 2K-output test, it ran at 27.71 ms per token (36.09 tokens per second). title: GaussianRenderFormer: Transformer-based Rendering of 3D Gaussian Splats
author: Shahaf Valencia Levy, Sagie Benaim
contentSnippet: Can a neural network learn to render 3D Gaussian splats on its own, with no rasterizer in the renderer? We present GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer that takes a set of Gaussians and a camera and outputs the image directly. Each Gaussian becomes one token in a view-independent encoder, and a view-dependent decoder turns small patches of camera rays into pixels by attending to those tokens. Trained on 26,820 Objaverse objects pruned to 20,000 Gaussians each, GaussianRenderFormer renders 300 unseen objects at 38.08 dB PSNR against the full, unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The gap is not one of generalization, and our diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder: telling it the projected footprint of each Gaussian, which it could in principle infer, adds 1.4 dB. Under-training is not ruled out. Code, trained models and videos: https://svlwoof.github.io/gaussianrenderformer

title: Soniox STT v6 Adds Agent Text Input and Echo Filtering for Voice Agents
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Soniox has released Soniox STT v6 , the latest generation of its speech-to-text API. Soniox STT v6 is a speech-to-text model that reads what a voice agent says while hearing the caller. It uses that text to recognize short replies and to drop the agent’s own voice. The release ships as stt-rt-v6 for streaming and stt-async-v6 for files , across 60+ languages. TL;DR Size: Soniox STT v6 is a proprietary hosted model, no parameter count published. Runs on: Soniox cloud API only (WebSocket streaming and async REST). No self-hosted or on-device option disclosed. Performance: Soniox calls it “significantly” more accurate than v5, but publishes no v6 numbers yet. Best: Price. $0.12/hour streaming and $0.10/hour async, with diarization and language ID bundled. Worst: Zero independent v6 results. Its v5 predecessor scored 1.34% semantic WER on Pipecat, behind v4’s 1.25%. What problem does Soniox STT v6 solve? In a cascaded voice agent, STT usually hears only the caller. It never sees the question being answered. Short answers suffer most. In Soniox’s docs , “River Roast” becomes “River Road” and “a tow” becomes “a tour.” The second problem is echo. Agent audio leaks back through speakerphones and laptops, gets transcribed as user speech, and the agent interrupts itself. How does agent text input work? You enable it with one flag in the start request: "enable_agent_text_input": true . It is only available on stt-rt-v6 , not the async model. While the agent speaks, you stream its words on the same WebSocket as the caller’s audio. Each message is a small JSON frame: {"type": "agent_text", "text": "...", "end_of_segment": true} . Timing matters. Messages carry no timestamps, so the model places text where it arrives in the audio stream. Soniox recommends sending each piece 500 ms to 1 second before playback, paced by TTS timestamps. On barge-in, you flush what was already played, send end_of_segment: true , and drop the unplayed rest. The agent’s text never appears in the returned transcript. How does agent voice echo cancellation work? With agent text input on, v6 knows what the agent is saying. It uses that to separate leftover agent audio from caller speech and filter it out. It keeps listening during playback, so callers can still interrupt. It does not replace acoustic echo cancellation. It handles what your existing AEC leaves behind , so keep AEC on. What else cha

title: Iterated creation, grading, and revision of data science projects by language models
author: Rohan Alexander
contentSnippet: We evaluate the extent to which agentic AI models can complete an end-to-end data science project, and how this improves with feedback. A 'writer' model with specific tools creates a complete data science project including downloading, cleaning, and analyzing a dataset, and writing a short paper about it. The project is executed and a 'grader' model evaluates it. The writer can then revise its submission, and this repeats for a total of three rounds. We consider seven models from five developers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and Z.AI. Each model is both a writer and a grader, so there are 49 writer-grader pairs and we run each pair three times. Of the 147 initial submissions, 107 run and render, and the average score increases from 59 per cent to 76 per cent after the final round of feedback. By writer the extent of the increase ranges from 3 percentage points for Anthropic's Opus 5.5 to 46 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5, and by grader it ranges from 13 percentage points for Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash to 32 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5. When a model grades its own writing the score tends to be about 9 percentage points higher than the average of what the other models give it. About half of the difference that we see from round to round is within the grader's own noise. Feedback generally results in the highest marks, but even just having the chance to revise, or having the additional budget, in terms of time or tool calls, without any feedback, results in considerable increases for some of the models but not for others. We find that how much such a loop helps depends on which model plays which role, but weaker models generally do not improve stronger models.

title: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges
author: Marina Temkin
contentSnippet: Posted: 11:34 AM PST · November 3, 2026 Image Credits: monsitj / Getty Images Marina Temkin AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges Fal , a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in it

summary.tldr:
San Francisco-based AI inference provider Fal has secured $1.3 billion in a Series F funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. This latest capital injection brings the company's valuation to $16 billion, doubling its $8 billion valuation from April 2026. The company simultaneously announced its Series E round, bringing the total capital raised across both rounds to $1.65 billion, with the earlier Series E led by Sequoia.

Fal specializes in hosting and executing AI video, image, and audio models, catering to a growing market of customers utilizing open-source models for production inference. The company has demonstrated significant commercial traction, reporting over $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year. Despite this growth, the broader inference sector—including competitors like Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal—faces structural challenges regarding thin gross margins, driven primarily by the high capital expenditure required to lease or purchase compute resources.

Founded in 2021 by former Coinbase machine learning leader Burkay Gur and former Amazon developer Gorkem Yurtseven, Fal is part of a wave of infrastructure startups benefiting from the surge in demand for scalable model deployment services.
takeaways: **Funding Totals:** Fal raised a combined $1.65 billion across Series E and F rounds, with the Series F alone contributing $1.3 billion.
**Valuation Growth:** The company's valuation reached $16 billion, a 2x increase from its $8 billion valuation recorded in April 2026.
**Revenue Milestone:** Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier in 2026.

**Market Context:** The inference sector faces thin gross margins due to the high costs of compute, despite rapid growth and high-valuation funding rounds for players like Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal.
**Leadership:** The company was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur (ex-Coinbase) and Gorkem Yurtseven (ex-Amazon).

title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence
author: Hao Fei
contentSnippet: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.

title: Netflix’s new AI Discover tab helps you find something to watch based on your mood
author: Aisha Malik
contentSnippet:
Netflix announced on Tuesday that it’s rolling out a new “AI Discover” tab where users will be able to experiment with new ways to find their next watch. The first experimental feature launching under the tab will allow users to get recommendations based on what they’re currently in the mood for.

Users can choose from curated themes featuring clips from shows and movies, based on their mood, viewing preferences, how much time they have, or what’s new and trending. Themes include “something light,” “scare me,” “family movie night,” “quick watches,” and more.

The addition of the new tab suggests that Netflix wants to make its growing library easier to navigate while shifting discovery away from an experience where users are endlessly scrolling through titles toward a more personalized and AI-powered experience.

Netflix says AI Discover is powered by a new intelligence layer it’s been building that responds to what users tell the platform in real time and keeps learning.

Once users pick a theme, they’ll see matching recommendations. They also have the option to select more specific themes so they can keep searching until they find something they’re interested in, or choose the “something different” option to start over. Each title features a “Tune Your Recommendations” button beside “Play” and “My List” to allow users to save recommendations they like or exclude titles they don’t want suggested again.

“There’s more to enjoy and discover on Netflix than ever, but what sounds right for a quiet night in may look different for family movie night or a few spare minutes,” Netflix wrote in a blog post . “We’ve spent years refining how you discover, with recommendations tailored to your tastes, from what you Thumbs Up to what you add to ‘My List.’ Now, AI Discover joins the mix as a new way to explore.”

Netflix describes AI Discover as its “test kitchen,” where it will “try out new recipes for discovery.” The company says users’ feedback will help it decide which features to keep or improve before bringing them over to the main Netflix experience.

AI Discover is starting to roll out in the U.S. to users who use Netflix in English on supported TVs. The company plans to bring the new tab to additional users in the coming weeks.

If users have access to the new feature, they’ll see a “Discover” button with a red gem icon and a “New” label in the top navigation bar

summary.tldr:
Netflix has introduced a new "AI Discover" tab, an experimental interface designed to replace traditional "endless scrolling" with a mood-based, interactive recommendation system. The feature is powered by a new intelligence layer that processes user input in real-time, allowing viewers to select curated themes such as "something light," "scare me," or "quick watches." Users can refine these suggestions through iterative prompts or by selecting a "something different" option to reset the discovery flow.

Beyond initial selection, the interface includes a "Tune Your Recommendations" button adjacent to the standard "Play" and "My List" controls. This allows users to explicitly save or exclude specific titles, providing a feedback loop that informs the underlying model. Netflix characterizes the AI Discover tab as a "test kitchen" for discovery features, where user engagement data will determine which tools are eventually integrated into the primary Netflix experience.

The feature is currently rolling out to English-language users in the U.S. on supported TV devices. Eligible users can access the tool via a "Discover" button marked with a red gem icon and a "New" label located in the top navigation bar.
takeaways: **Interface Access:** The feature is identified by a red gem icon and a "New" label in the top navigation bar on supported TV devices.
**Feedback Mechanism:** A "Tune Your Recommendations" button allows users to manually save or exclude titles to influence future suggestions.
**Core Functionality:** The system uses a real-time intelligence layer to filter content based on mood, viewing preferences, time availability, and trending status.
**Deployment Scope:** Currently limited to U.S. users with English-language settings on supported TVs, with a broader rollout planned for the coming weeks.

title: Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: Starting today, Siri can tune into the Apple Watch’s mic with Audio Intelligence features that are available in the new watchOS 27.3 developer beta rolling out now. The two new additions are Siri Recap, which uses “ambient listening” to generate summaries of your conversation, and Live Rewind, which generates text transcripts of the last 15 seconds of audio your watch’s mic detected. Apple is also releasing its redesigned Health app for testing today in the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and announced expanded language support in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese. It adds sections like a new Insights tab with summaries for heart, sleep, fitness, and other data that pop up during the day, a For You section with personalized recommendations, and health content like educational videos and articles. Apple: * Live Rewind, which can help users recall what was just said in conversation. A double-press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so the user can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with. Users can ask Siri about the content of the text or save it to the Siri app to revisit later. * Siri Recap, which can create high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment. When it comes to the implications of an ambient, always-listening AI, Apple has released this Audio Intelligence Privacy Overview (pdf) about how it plans to protect users’ privacy when their watch is listening around the clock. It goes into detail about Apple’s claims that users’ raw audio “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.” According to Apple, “If you use iCloud with two-factor authentication and have a device passcode, any Siri Recap summary or Live Rewind text snippet you choose to save syncs across your devices end-to-end encrypted in the Siri app.”

summary.tldr:
Apple has introduced new 'Audio Intelligence' features for the Apple Watch via the watchOS 27.3 developer beta. The update includes two primary tools: Siri Recap, which utilizes ambient listening to generate conversation summaries, and Live Rewind, which provides a 15-second text transcript of recent audio captured by the watch microphone. These features are designed to assist with memory recall and conversation engagement, with users able to trigger Live Rewind via a double-press of the Digital Crown.

Alongside the watchOS update, Apple released an iOS 27.3 developer beta featuring a redesigned Health app. This app includes a new 'Insights' tab for heart, sleep, and fitness data, a 'For You' section for personalized recommendations, and educational health content. The update expands language support to include global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

To address privacy concerns regarding always-on ambient listening, Apple published an Audio Intelligence Privacy Overview. The company claims raw audio is processed exclusively within dedicated hardware, is never saved as a file, and remains inaccessible to the operating system or third-party apps. Saved summaries and transcripts are end-to-end encrypted and synced across devices via iCloud for users with two-factor authentication and a device passcode.
takeaways: **Live Rewind Functionality:** Users can double-press the Digital Crown to view a 15-second text transcript of recent audio, which can be queried via Siri or saved to the Siri app.
**Siri Recap Architecture:** The feature automatically generates titles and key points from conversations, storing them in the Siri app for later review.
**Privacy Infrastructure:** Apple states that raw audio is processed in dedicated hardware and is not accessible to the OS or apps, with saved data protected by end-to-end encryption.
**Health App Redesign:** The iOS 27.3 beta introduces an Insights tab for daily health metrics and a For You section for personalized recommendations.

**Language Expansion:** The new features support 10 languages, including global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

title: OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
author: Hayden Field
contentSnippet: In many circles, “Ask Chat” has replaced “Google it,” and that’s reflected in a new announcement from OpenAI: the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google. Adam Fry, OpenAI’s consumer product lead for ChatGPT, made the announcement at a press event on Monday. He said the company defines a search as any time a user inputs a query that results in a web search, as opposed to tasks like defining a term or a simple how-to explanation. (Fry did not specify the source of the Google search volume number.) Having one-fifth as many searches as Google is still a long way from overtaking it, but for comparison, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during Google’s 2023 antitrust trial that Bing had about 3 percent of the search engine market share after trying for more than a decade. During the trial, Google described AI as a potential disruptor, arguing ChatGPT was poised to seriously compete with it — now, OpenAI seems to agree. (OpenAI likely uses Microsoft Bing for a significant part of its searches, along with its in-house search index, although there is still some speculation that it routes some queries through Google.) The news comes amid an ongoing search engine shake-up, as Google continues to reduce conventional referrals to third-party sites and invests heavily in AI tools — not just AI Overview but also additional generative AI capabilities, including personalized search results with visualizations and charts. But as search queries increasingly route through OpenAI and other AI labs’ services, other companies are investing in the same types of AI-focused search experience, even if they call it something else: for OpenAI, it’s “Intelligent UI,” or creating a visual and interactive interface within a chatbot response. “That’s where the future of this technology goes. You’re talking to a canvas,” Fry said. Much like Google, OpenAI sees a potential path to profitability through ads, particularly as it approaches an IPO potentially slated for early next year. OpenAI has defended its ads in the past, and Fry told reporters they hadn’t produced a lasting backlash. “Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product,” he said, adding that “most people do not seem to mind ads in the product.” OpenAI announced last month that the company would begin introducing images of sponsored products and

summary.tldr:
OpenAI’s consumer product lead, Adam Fry, announced that ChatGPT’s search query volume has reached 20 percent of Google’s total search volume. OpenAI defines these search queries as inputs requiring a web search, excluding simple definitions or how-to explanations. While the specific methodology for calculating Google’s search volume was not disclosed, this metric highlights a significant shift in user behavior compared to Microsoft Bing, which held approximately 3 percent market share after over a decade of operation, as cited during Google’s 2023 antitrust trial.

OpenAI is positioning its search experience as an "Intelligent UI," moving toward an interactive, canvas-based interface rather than traditional link-based results. The company continues to rely on a combination of Microsoft Bing and its own in-house search index to power these queries. As OpenAI approaches a potential IPO in early 2025, it is actively expanding its advertising strategy. Fry noted that the introduction of sponsored product images has not caused user backlash, and the company is exploring ways to increase ad integration within the platform.
takeaways: **Search Volume:** ChatGPT search queries now reach 20 percent of the volume processed by Google.
**Market Context:** Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella previously testified that Bing held only 3 percent market share after more than 10 years of development.
**Ad Strategy:** OpenAI is transitioning from simple text/logo-based ads to sponsored product images, with leadership suggesting potential for further ad expansion.
**Interface Philosophy:** OpenAI describes its search evolution as an "Intelligent UI" or "canvas," focusing on visual and interactive responses rather than traditional search referrals.

title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
author: Kewei Zhang, Juncheng Ma, Guodong Lv, Duomin Wang
contentSnippet: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus 5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs 107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \117 for teleoperation in China and below 290 in labour alone in North America.

title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
author: Minsoo Cheong, Sungjoo Yoo
contentSnippet: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose LoopVQ, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to 4.3times and 6.1times on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.

title: Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up
author: Jay Peters
contentSnippet: Many indie game developers have recently posted on social media about unexpectedly long approval wait times for their game submissions on Steam, with some of the approvals causing developers to miss their planned launch dates. For example, Studio Daimon, the team behind an upcoming title called Food Devils, had planned to launch the game in early access today after submitting its build on October 12th. But the game is “still awaiting approval,” according to a post from game director Alfred Kamon. “Even now, we don’t know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game. We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored.” In October, publisher 2 Left Thumbs said it missed its planned launch of Wheel Make It “by nearly two weeks” due to the long wait for build reviews. You can read some details about the studio’s setbacks, including failing a review for a “one single option in the menu” not being accessible with a controller, in a Steam post. There are lots of other recent posts about review build waits as well. Valve says on a Steam developer website that a review of a game’s store presence “typically takes 3-5 business days to complete,” though the company suggests submitting a page for review “at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.” However, as of late, Steam has seemingly been grappling with a sharp increase in games; October’s Steam Next Fest had 7,240 games, a 65.2 percent increase over June’s Steam Next Fest, according to How to Market a Game. A Reddit user also found that 49.9 percent of all games released since Valve started asking developers in 2024 to label games that use AI now have an AI disclosure. Kamon and 2 Left Thumbs suspect the longer waits are due to “slop” slowing down the process. “We can only assume it’s because Steam’s review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers,” said Kamon. Valve didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. Itch.io has also been dealing with a rise in games, with the platform saying last weekend that “The number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past 2 months.” Last night, the platform said it “Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌”

summary.tldr:
Indie game developers are reporting significant delays in Steam's build approval process, causing multiple studios to miss their scheduled launch dates. Studio Daimon, developers of 'Food Devils,' submitted their build on October 12th and remained in the review queue past their intended early access launch date, despite filing urgent support tickets. Similarly, publisher 2 Left Thumbs reported a two-week delay for their title 'Wheel Make It,' citing the review backlog as the primary cause for missing their release window.

While Valve’s official documentation states that store presence reviews typically take 3-5 business days, developers suggest the actual wait time has extended to several weeks. Industry observers attribute this bottleneck to a surge in submissions, evidenced by the October Steam Next Fest featuring 7,240 games—a 65.2% increase over the June event. Developers and publishers speculate that the influx of AI-generated content, or "slop," is clogging the review queue. This trend is corroborated by data showing that 49.9% of games released in 2024 include AI disclosures. Other platforms are facing similar pressures; Itch.io recently reported that daily game page creation has doubled in the last two months, leading the platform to delete terabytes of AI-generated content.
takeaways: **Submission Volume:** Steam Next Fest saw 7,240 games in October, representing a 65.2% increase in volume compared to the June event.
**AI Prevalence:** 49.9% of all games released on Steam in 2024 have included an AI disclosure label.
**Official Guidelines:** Valve officially advises developers to submit store pages for review at least 7 business days before a planned launch to account for potential feedback.
**Platform Strain:** Itch.io reported that the number of new game pages created per day has doubled over the past two months, prompting the deletion of terabytes of AI-generated content.

title: Netflix will show you themed recommendations through a new ‘AI Discover’ tab
author: Jay Peters
contentSnippet: Netflix’s TV app is getting a new “AI Discover” tab where the company will show experimental, AI-powered features to help you find new shows and movies to watch. The first of these experiments surfaces content based around themes, like “Something Light,” “Family Movie Night,” or “Quick Watches.” When you pick a theme, Netflix will show you recommendations that match it. If you don’t like a recommendation, you can tell that to Netflix, and the app will remember it. The company says that AI Discover is powered by “a new intelligence layer we’ve been building that responds to what members tell us in real time and keeps learning.” AI Discover, which will show up as a “Discover” tab along your top menu, is gradually starting to roll out in the US to “members who use Netflix in English on supported TVs.” The announcement follows Netflix recently laying off around 1,000 employees as growth has slowed and users are reportedly watching the service less.

summary.tldr:
Netflix is introducing a new "AI Discover" tab on its TV app, designed to surface experimental, AI-powered content recommendations. The initial feature groups recommendations around specific themes such as "Something Light," "Family Movie Night," and "Quick Watches." Users can provide real-time feedback on recommendations they dislike, which the app stores to refine future suggestions.

According to Netflix, the system is driven by a newly constructed intelligence layer engineered to adapt dynamically to user input and learn continuously. The feature will appear as a "Discover" tab in the top menu and is currently rolling out gradually to English-language users on supported televisions in the US.

The rollout coincides with broader organizational changes at Netflix, following recent layoffs of approximately 1,000 employees amid slowing subscriber growth and declining viewing metrics.
takeaways: **New Feature Location:** The experimental tab is designated as "AI Discover" and will appear as a "Discover" option along the top menu of the Netflix TV app.
**Initial Themes:** The first wave of theme-based recommendations includes categories such as "Something Light," "Family Movie Night," and "Quick Watches."
**Feedback Mechanism:** Users can signal dislike for specific recommendations, and the application retains this feedback to adapt future suggestions.
**Underlying Architecture:** Netflix states the feature runs on a newly built intelligence layer designed to respond to real-time member input and learn continuously.

**Rollout Scope:** The feature is gradually deploying to English-language users on supported TVs in the United States, arriving shortly after Netflix laid off around 1,000 employees due to slowing growth and viewing hours.

title: Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick
author: Puneeth Komaragiri
contentSnippet: Organizations collect data in many forms. Structured data lives in databases and spreadsheets, whereas unstructured data sits in documents, reports, and files stored across file systems. Analyzing both together typically requires switching between multiple tools, running separate queries, and manually correlating results. Amazon Quick addresses this with a unified experience. You can connect structured data through enriched datasets and unstructured data through S3-backed knowledge bases . You can then query both through a single conversational AI agent. In this post, you learn how to: Connect Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) as a data source and create a knowledge base. Build a Space that combines structured and unstructured data. Create and configure a custom chat agent that queries across both data types. Ask questions that span structured and unstructured sources in a single conversation. Solution architecture The following diagram illustrates how each component connects to deliver a unified data experience through Amazon Quick. Figure 1: Solution architecture for combining structured and unstructured data in Amazon Quick The architecture has three layers: Data layer: Your data exists in two forms. Unstructured content (documents, PDFs, reports) is stored in Amazon S3 and indexed through a knowledge base. Structured data (metrics, sales figures, and operational key performance indicators) is loaded as enriched datasets with semantic descriptions that the agent uses to translate questions into SQL. Workspace layer: A Space brings both data types together into a single workspace. The Space references your knowledge base for unstructured queries and your datasets for structured queries. It can also include dashboards, file uploads, and action connectors. This is the layer where data from different sources converges into a unified context. Agent layer: The custom chat agent links to the Space and uses it as its knowledge source. When a user asks a question, the agent determines whether to query the knowledge base, the dataset, or both, and returns a combined response with citations. title: ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
author: Greg Biegel
contentSnippet: AI agents that interact with enterprise APIs on behalf of users need to maintain user identity throughout the request chain. Without identity propagation, API calls arrive at downstream services as the application itself rather than the user who initiated the action. This breaks audit trails, bypasses user-level access controls, and violates the principle of least privilege. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post shows how to configure AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID. An AI agent can then call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user’s identity. You configure the token exchange on the gateway target, and AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange on each request. The pattern can be applied to other REST APIs protected by OAuth. In production, you can additionally pair identity propagation with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful content and validate the agent’s inputs and outputs. Solution overview The architecture involves three key components connected through AgentCore Gateway: An AI agent application, protected by Microsoft Entra ID through an OAuth application registration. A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, implemented using AgentCore Gateway, sitting between the agent and ServiceNow. The ServiceNow REST API, configured with an inbound OAuth integration tied to Microsoft Entra ID. The following figure shows the end-to-end solution architecture, including components within AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow. Figure 1: Solution architecture across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow As shown in Figure 1, the user acquires a JSON Web Token (JWT) to invoke the agent 1. The agent authenticates to the gateway with a JWT token scoped to the agent’s own application registration 2. The gateway then exchanges that token, using the OBO flow, for a new token scoped to the ServiceNow API connector, with the original user’s identity preserved 3. ServiceNow receives a valid token whose preferred_username claim maps to an existing ServiceNow user and applies that user’s permissions to the API call 4. title: How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search
author: Iskander Sanchez-Rola
contentSnippet: Your professional reputation now lives online first. Recruiters check LinkedIn before returning a call. Clients review your digital presence before booking a first meeting. For ambitious professionals, that shift is an opportunity: a well-crafted online voice can open doors that a résumé alone never could. But standing out takes more than content generation. It takes real-time awareness of what’s happening right now. A professional building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader needs to react to today’s breakthroughs, not last week’s headlines. And with feeds flooded by AI-generated noise, audiences reward authenticity and timeliness more than ever. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore made that possible. We built Norton Revamp , a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform. At its heart is an AI-curated News Engine, powered by AgentCore Web Search, that grounds every content suggestion, goal recommendation, and news feed item in current, cited web knowledge. The platform launched in March 2026, built by a small group of engineers. In this post, we show you how the Gen team builds an AI-curated News Engine in Norton Revamp with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search to help customers turn ideas into engaging social media posts. The challenge: Real-time grounding for professional content Unlike chatbots that rely on static knowledge bases, Norton Revamp needs to understand what’s trending right now in each user’s professional domain. A cyber security expert needs today’s threat intelligence. A marketing leader needs this week’s industry shifts. Traditional approaches (custom web crawlers, third-party news APIs, static content databases) each carry trade-offs: infrastructure overhead, stale data, vendor complexity, or data egress risk. We evaluated three alternatives before choosing AgentCore Web Search. Custom crawlers require ongoing maintenance and lag real time. Third-party news APIs added vendor contracts, API key management, and data leaving our AWS environment. Static knowledge bases were perpetually stale. AgentCore Web Search eliminated these concerns. It’s fully managed with zero infrastructure overhead, operates entirely within AWS with zero data egress, and returns cited sources with URLs and publication dates. title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Rajesh Nagpal
contentSnippet: In this post, we show how to build a semantic layer for agentic AI using EDB Postgres AI . We run a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that queries the layer to answer customer 360 (C360) questions. Earlier posts in this series built the same C360 pattern with Stardog’s knowledge graph , Denodo’s data virtualization platform , AtScale’s dimensional model , and Strategy Mosaic’s linked models . EDB Postgres AI puts the semantic layer inside the operational Postgres database as an AIDB extension . Business meaning lives next to the data in standard Postgres COMMENT statements, the join graph comes from Postgres foreign keys, and governance uses Postgres GRANT and row-level security through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that ships with AIDB. By the end of this post you will know: How to build an AIDB semantic knowledge base (SemKB) over a Postgres schema, how COMMENT ON statements and aidb.create_semantic_alias behave as the authoring surface, and how foreign keys crawl into join paths. How to expose the AIDB tool catalog to an external agent through the built-in EDB MCP endpoint, fronted by an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and registered as an MCP target on AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. How Postgres roles, column-level GRANT statements, and row-level security produce different results for different callers. The prompt, tool catalog, and agent code stay the same. How AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for every SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, queryable with ordinary SQL. Three layers an agent needs An agent that answers business questions from live data needs three layers: a model that plans and writes queries, a meaning layer that tells the agent what the data represents, and a runtime that hosts the agent and controls identity and access. The Stardog post in this series introduced this framing. The model layer in this post is Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock , the same as prior posts (model availability varies by AWS Region ). The runtime layer is AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore Gateway handles inbound authorization, and AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, holds outbound credentials for the tool targets, same as prior posts. title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
author: Nolan Chen
contentSnippet: Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide. Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking. This post introduces how Cartesia , an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation. The rise of conversational AI and latency expectations The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries: Contact centers: AI agents handling millions of customer interactions require instantaneous speech generation to maintain natural dialogue. Telehealth: Remote patient consultations demand low-latency voice for accurate, empathetic communication. Gaming and virtual worlds: Immersive experiences require real-time voice synthesis for non-player characters (NPCs) and player interactions. Accessibility: Screen readers and voice interfaces must respond instantly to serve users with visual impairments. Inbound and outbound sales: AI sales agents must respond without awkward pauses to qualify leads, handle objections, and keep prospects on the line. Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off. AI for voice: State Space Models (SSM) State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. title: Introducing India-based inference for Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock
author: Naomi Teng
contentSnippet: Kimi K3 is a multi-modal, open-weight foundation model (FM) that provider Moonshot AI reported achieved frontier-level coding and general agentic intelligence at release. In addition to global and US-based inference, Amazon Bedrock now supports in-country inference in India for Kimi K3: unblocking local workloads with strict data residency requirements. Customers like Ultrahuman are already seeing the benefits in production: “Jade, an AI Health and Wellness assistant in the Ultrahuman app, answers questions in plain language using each person’s own Ring and glucose data, across more than 14,000 conversations a day. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock let us add a leading open-weight model through the API we already use, with health data staying inside AWS and Mumbai as a fallback Region. With prompt caching, we’ve cut LLM costs by 80 percent and made multi-turn chats 85 percent faster.” — Aditya Patawari, VP Engineering, Ultrahuman In this post, we explain the different global and geographic inference options available, and share code for an example use case: optical character recognition (OCR) and understanding of Indic-language documents, with follow-up question answering in code-mixed Hinglish. Choose where inference can run Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock is offered through cross-Region inference profiles . You can invoke the model from any of a wide range of AWS Regions (the “source”). Amazon Bedrock then securely processes your request in one of multiple possible “destination” Regions. Cross-Region inference is fully managed by AWS: Data is encrypted in transit between Regions and remains on the AWS network, never traversing the public internet or requiring you to set up any multi-Region virtual private cloud (VPC) infrastructure. title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. title: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: In 2023, malware tracked as BlackLotus became the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. With the industry-wide chain-of-trust mechanism subverted, the malware was able to run malicious code before Windows was fully loaded and many security defenses were operational. Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability that BlackLotus exploited in 2022. In 2023 and 2024, Microsoft issued additional updates. The first added a new certificate that no longer trusted the vulnerable boot managers. The second provided the means to revoke trust in the digital certificate used to sign older vulnerable Windows boot managers. The organizations infected by the new bootkit, which is tracked under the name BlackX, had installed all of these patches. So how did they fall victim? UEFI bootkit refresher Before discussing the incident further, a brief review of BlackLotus and UEFI malware is in order. Short for Unified Extensible Firmware Interface , UEFI is firmware that runs immediately after a computer is turned on. One of its main jobs is to load system configuration settings, identify and initialize hardware components, and prepare the computer to start its OS. Read full article Comments

title: AI Is Changing How Semiconductor Fabs Work — and Engineers Are Moving Faster Because of It
author: Timothy Costa
contentSnippet: Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking. For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences. AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast. Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials. Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time. AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours. And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. This helps engineers optimize equipment and processes, compare alternatives and decide which changes to test physically. By integrating NVIDIA cuDSS, Applied’s Ginestra simulation platform runs up to 10x faster than CPU-only approaches. Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking.

For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences.

title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
author: Oswaldo Ludwig
contentSnippet: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.

title: How a Kenyan Startup Is Rethinking AI for Small Businesses
author: Lucila Pinto
contentSnippet: The first time Mutembei Kariuki thought about how AI models could work in Kenya, his home country, was in 2019. He was attending a conference at the University of Tokyo on the future of AI, and kept hearing about how this technology was going to transform the world. “But nobody mentioned Africa at all,” he says. Even then—before AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic had launched their chatbots to the public—Kariuki could see significant obstacles to AI adoption in Africa. Internet access was slow and unequal, computing resources for training models were scarce, and there was little high-quality, structured training data. Most people, meanwhile, reached the internet through outdated, low-memory cellphones rather than computers or high-end phones. Together with cofounders Jude Mwenda and Stephanie Njerenga , Kariuki created Fastagger , a startup that builds AI models that can run offline and on low-power cellphones. Its first big product, Auni, is a business-intelligence assistant that launched in 2024; it got a big push when it was integrated into the business app of M-Pesa , Kenya’s largest mobile money service. Since then, about 6,000 businesses have signed up. Auni helps small and medium businesses like barbershops, restaurants, and small manufacturers analyze their transaction data and gives them marketing recommendations. Peter Chege, owner of a salon and barbershop in Nairobi, started using Auni last year. Before that, he recorded all his sales on paper. “We were not able to translate that information into a graph,” he says. Now, the app helps him identify his busiest days and hours, as well as his loyal customers. If a regular customer stops coming, for example, he can send a personalized message encouraging them to return. Fastagger is part of an emerging effort to build AI around the technological realities of users in developing economies, rather than adapting products designed for wealthier markets. In Fastagger’s case, that meant finding a way to make their models work despite inexpensive phones, unreliable internet connections, and business records that may consist of little more than mobile-money transactions. title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
author: Carlos Hartmann
contentSnippet: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.
